Instead, the overhead of model parallelism\\\\n(§3.3) starts to become a signiﬁcant factor.\\\\nThe mean and P99 latency results of changing CV are in\\\\nFig. 6. With a higher CV, the requests become more bursty,\\\\n4\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 5 ===\\\\n5\\\\n10\\\\n15\\\\n20\\\\nSLO Scale\\\\n0\\\\n50\\\\n100\\\\nSLO Attainment (%)\\\\nModel Parallelism\\\\nReplication\\\\n(a) Real model latency.\\\\n5\\\\n10\\\\n15\\\\n20\\\\nSLO Scale\\\\n0\\\\n50\\\\n100\\\\nSLO Attainment (%)\\\\nModel Parallelism ( =1.0)\\\\nModel Parallelism ( =1.1)\\\\nModel Parallelism ( =1.2)\\\\nModel Parallelism ( =1.3)\\\\nModel Parallelism ( =1.4)\\\\nModel Parallelism ( =1.5)\\\\nReplication\\\\n(b) Changing overhead.\\\\nFigure 7: SLO attainment with changing SLOs. For example,\\\\nadvertising systems may choose not to show an ad rather\\\\nthan delay rendering user content. In this case, the goal of the\\\\nserving system is to optimize the percentage of requests that\\\\ncan be ﬁnished within the deadline, i.e., SLO attainment.\\\\nIn this experiment, we measure how SLOs affect the perfor-\\\\nmance of the placement methods. We compare the replication\\\\nand the model-parallel placement with 8-stage pipeline par-\\\\nallelism. During execution, we drop the requests that will\\\\nexceed the deadline even if we schedule it immediately. We\\\\nscale the SLO to different multiplies of the single device exe-\\\\ncution latency (SLO Scale in Fig. 7a) and compare the SLO\\\\nattainment of the two methods.\\\\nAs in Fig. 7a, when SLO is tight, model parallelism can\\\\ngreatly improve SLO attainment. However, when the SLO\\\\nbecomes looser, its SLO attainment plateaus but that of the\\\\nreplication placement keeps growing. This result shares the\\\\nsame core logic as previous experiments: When SLO be-\\\\ncomes looser, more requests can stay in the waiting queue,\\\\nand thus the effective burstiness of the requests decreases.\\\\nWhen many requests are queued, the system is bounded by\\\\nits total processing capability, which might be affected by the\\\\nmodel parallelism overhead.\\\\nSummary: Model parallelism beneﬁts model serving\\\\nthrough statistical multiplexing when the device mem-\\\\nory is limited, the request rate is low, the request CV is\\\\nhigh, or the SLO is tight.\\\\n3.3\\\\nOverhead of Model Parallelism\\\\nIn this section, we further investigate the overheads of dif-\\\\nferent model parallel strategies and how they affect serving\\\\nperformance. Similar to the setup in Fig. 7a, we manually\\\\nmodify the overhead of model parallelism. Speciﬁcally, let\\\\nthe latency of a single model executing on the GPU be L and\\\\nthe number of pipeline stages be n. We set the total latency of\\\\npipeline execution to be αL and the latency of each pipeline\\\\nstage to be αL/n, where α is a parameter that controls the\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\nNumber of GPUs\\\\n0.0\\\\n0.1\\\\n0.2\\\\n0.3\\\\nLatency (s)\\\\nCompuation\\\\nCommunication Overhead\\\\nUneven Partition Overhead\\\\n(a) Inter-op parallelism.\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\nNumber of GPUs\\\\n0.00\\\\n0.05\\\\n0.10\\\\n0.15\\\\n0.20\\\\n0.25\\\\nLatency (s)\\\\nCompuation\\\\nCommunication Overhead\\\\n(b) Intra-op parallelism.\\\\nFigure 8: The overhead decomposition. The overhead of inter-\\\\nop parallelism mainly comes from uneven partition while the\\\\noverhead of intra-op parallelism comes from communication.\\\\noverhead. When α = 1, model parallelism does not have any\\\\noverhead and larger α means higher overhead.\\\\nWe show the results in Fig. 7b. If model parallelism does\\\\nnot have any overhead (α = 1), it can always outperform repli-\\\\ncation due to its ability to multiplex the devices. When the\\\\noverhead becomes larger and the SLO is low, model paral-\\\\nlelism still outperforms replication. However, with a larger\\\\nSLO, the effective burstiness is reduced and the performance\\\\nis dominated by the overhead.\\\\nGiven that the overhead can greatly affect serving perfor-\\\\nmance, we perform a detailed study of the multiple sources\\\\nof model-parallel overhead in Fig. 8. For inter-op parallelism,\\\\nwhen partitioning a single model into multiple stages, dif-\\\\nferent stages need to communicate the intermediate tensors,\\\\nand we denote this overhead as the communication overhead.\\\\nIn addition, the pipeline execution will be bottlenecked by\\\\nthe execution time of the slowest stage, making the effective\\\\nlatency to be the number of pipeline stages times the latency\\\\nof the slowest stage [19]. We denote this as the uneven par-\\\\ntition overhead. As in Fig. 8a, for inter-op parallelism, most\\\\noverhead comes from the latency imbalance among differ-\\\\nent pipeline stages, instead of the communication between\\\\nstages. While our previous discussion mainly focus on inter-\\\\nop parallelism, the other type of model parallelism, intra-op\\\\nparallelism, has very different performance characteristics. Its\\\\noverhead is merely brought by the collective communication\\\\nacross multiple devices [27]. From Fig. 8b, we can see that\\\\nthe communication overhead of intra-op parallelism is much\\\\nhigher than inter-op parallelism.\\\\nFinally, we compare the latency, throughput, and memory\\\\nconsumption of different model-parallel placements and the\\\\nreplication placement in Fig. 9. Because of the sequential\\\\ndependence between the different stages, inter-op parallelism\\\\ncannot reduce the execution latency of a single input data. In-\\\\nstead, the latency is slightly higher due to the communication\\\\nbetween the stages. On the other hand, intra-op parallelism\\\\ncan largely reduce the latency via the parallel execution of dif-\\\\nferent GPUs (Fig. 9a). However, because inter-op parallelism\\\\ncan pipeline the execution of different stages and only com-\\\\nmunicate a relatively small amount of data, it attains higher\\\\nthroughput compared to intra-op parallelism (Fig. 9b). Be-\\\\ncause both parallel methods split the model weight tensors\\\\n5\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 6 ===\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n6\\\\n8\\\\n#GPUs\\\\n0.0\\\\n0.1\\\\n0.2\\\\nLatency (s)\\\\nInter-op Parallelism\\\\nIntra-op Parallelism\\\\nReplication\\\\n(a) Single input latency.\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n6\\\\n8\\\\n#GPUs\\\\n10\\\\n20\\\\n30\\\\nThroughput (req/s)\\\\nInter-op Parallelism\\\\nIntra-op Parallelism\\\\nReplication\\\\n(b) Throughput.\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n6\\\\n8\\\\n#GPUs\\\\n10\\\\n20\\\\n30\\\\n40\\\\nMemory (GB)\\\\nInter-op Parallelism\\\\nIntra-op Parallelism\\\\nReplication\\\\n(c) Total memory usage.\\\\nFigure 9: The latency, throughput and memory usage vs. #GPUs for inter-op parallelism, intra-op parallelism, and replication.\\\\nacross different GPUs, the total memory usage stays con-\\\\nstant with increasing numbers of GPUs (Fig. 9c). This makes\\\\nthe statistical multiplexing of different GPUs across multiple\\\\nmodels possible.\\\\nIn the end, the tradeoff between parallelization strategies\\\\nand their interplay with cluster resources, arrival patterns, and\\\\nserving objectives forms an intricate design space.\\\\n3.4\\\\nQueueing Theory Analysis\\\\nIn this section, we use queuing theory to mathematically ver-\\\\nify the conclusions in §3.2 and §3.3. Speciﬁcally, we analyze\\\\nthe case where the inputs follow the Poisson arrival process.\\\\nSince the execution time of a deep learning inference task is\\\\nhighly predictable [17], we assume the request serving time is\\\\ndeterministic. For the single device case, suppose the request\\\\nrate to a model is λ0 and the single device latency is D with\\\\nthe utilization λ0D < 1, then the average number of requests\\\\nLQ and the average latency W in this M/D/1 queue [41] are:\\\\nLQ =\\\\nλ0D\\\\n2(1−λ0D),\\\\nW = D+LQD = D+\\\\nλ0D2\\\\n2(1−λ0D).\\\\nNow consider the example in §3.1. Let pλ,(1−p)λ be the\\\\naverage request rates for the two models respectively, where\\\\np ∈[0,1] controls the percentage of requests for both models.\\\\nThen for the simple placement, the average latency can be\\\\nderived as the average latency of two independent queues:\\\\nWsimple = D+\\\\np2λD2\\\\n2(1−pλD) +\\\\n(1−p)2λD2\\\\n2(1−(1−p)λD).\\\\nNote that Wsimple reaches minimum when p = 1/2. Intuitively,\\\\nwhen p is not exactly half, one model receives more requests\\\\nthan the other. This larger portion of requests have a longer\\\\nqueueing delay, which leads to the higher overall mean la-\\\\ntency.\\\\nFor the model-parallel case, the requests to both models\\\\nmerged to a single Poisson Process with rate λ. For pipeline\\\\nparallelism, suppose the latency for a single input to be Ds\\\\nand the maximum stage latency to be Dm, then the average\\\\nlatency would be\\\\nWpipeline = Ds +\\\\nλD2\\\\nm\\\\n2(1−λDm).\\\\n0.0\\\\n0.5\\\\n1.0\\\\n1.5\\\\n2.0\\\\nD\\\\n1.0\\\\n1.2\\\\n1.4\\\\nFigure 10: Maximal communication overhead α and uneven\\\\npartition overhead β satisfy Wpipeline ≤Wsimple as a function\\\\nof total utilization λD.\\\\nSuppose there is no model-parallel overhead, then Ds =\\\\n2Dm = D. Let’s ﬁrst consider the case where p = 1/2 (Fig. 2a).\\\\nWe have\\\\nWsimple = D+\\\\nλD2\\\\n4−2λD,\\\\nWpipeline = D+\\\\nλD2\\\\n8−4λD.\\\\nIn this case, the waiting time for model-parallel execution is\\\\nhalf of the simple placement waiting time, as shown in the\\\\nvertical lines in Fig. 2a. When the p is not 1/2, Wsimple will\\\\nincrease while Wpipeline will stay the same, so the gap between\\\\nWsimple and Wpipeline will be even larger, as in Fig. 2c.\\\\nNext, we consider the case where model parallelism in-\\\\ncurs overhead. We measure the two types of overheads in\\\\n§3.3 separately: With the overhead from communication,\\\\nDs = 2Dm = αD, where α ≥1 is the overhead factor. With\\\\nthe overhead from uneven stages, we suppose Ds = D still\\\\nholds, but Dm = βD/2 where β ≥1 is the overhead factor.\\\\nTo keep Wpipeline ≤Wsimple, we can get the maximal α and\\\\nβ as a function of the total utilization λD separately and we\\\\nvisualize the function in Fig. 10. When the utilization is high,\\\\nthe beneﬁt of statistical multiplexing diminishes, and thus\\\\nthe overhead needs to be low, as in §3.2. On the other hand,\\\\nwhen the utilization is very low, most requests will not be\\\\nqueued, and thus the communication overhead α needs to\\\\nbe low to keep the processing latency to be low. Note that\\\\nthe maximal overhead here is based on a uniform Poisson ar-\\\\nrival distribution. A more bursty or more non-uniform arrival\\\\ndistribution will make the simple placement performs worse\\\\nand make the model-parallelism placement outperforms the\\\\nsimple replication placement with even higher overhead.\\\\n4\\\\nMethod\\\\nFrom §3, we can see that there are several key challenges to\\\\neffectively utilize model parallelism for deep learning serving:\\\\n6\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 7 ===\\\\nController\\\\nHTTP Requests\\\\nModel a\\\\nModel b\\\\nModel c\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nModel Parallel Runtime\\\\nModel a\\\\nModel d\\\\nModel e\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nModel Parallel Runtime\\\\nModel f\\\\nModel g\\\\nGPU\\\\nGPU\\\\nModel Parallel Runtime\\\\nGroup 1\\\\nGroup 2\\\\nGroup 3\\\\nFigure 11: AlpaServe Runtime System Architecture\\\\n• Derive efﬁcient model parallel strategies for inference to\\\\nreduce the overhead of model parallelism. Speciﬁcally,\\\\nﬁnd a partitioning strategy that minimizes the stage im-\\\\nbalance for inter-operator parallelism.\\\\n• Determine model-parallel placements according to the\\\\narrival pattern to maximize SLO attainment.\\\\nWe built AlpaServe to speciﬁcally tackle these challenges.\\\\nThe runtime architecture of AlpaServe is shown in Fig. 11. Al-\\\\npaServe utilizes a centralized controller to dispatch requests to\\\\ndifferent groups. Each group hosts several model replicas on\\\\na shared model-parallel runtime. This section describes the ar-\\\\nchitecture of AlpaServe and the key algorithms for efﬁciently\\\\nleveraging model parallelism in a model serving system.\\\\n4.1\\\\nAutomatic Parallelization for Inference\\\\nSince different parallelization conﬁgurations have different\\\\nlatency and throughput trade-offs, we need to enumerate mul-\\\\ntiple possible conﬁgurations for every single model and let the\\\\nplacement algorithm choose the best combination for all mod-\\\\nels in the whole cluster. Therefore, given a model, AlpaServe\\\\nﬁrst runs an auto-parallelization compiler with various con-\\\\nstraints to generate a list of possible conﬁgurations. We build\\\\nseveral extensions on top of an existing auto parallelization\\\\ntraining system, Alpa [48], to make it suitable for generating\\\\nserving parallelization strategies. Alpa includes two passes\\\\nfor generating efﬁcient model parallel partitions: inter-op pass\\\\nand intra-op pass. The inter-op pass uses a dynamic program-\\\\nming (DP) algorithm to ﬁgure out the optimal inter-op parallel\\\\nplan, and it calls the intra-op pass for each potential pipeline\\\\nstage, which is formulated as an integer linear programming\\\\n(ILP) problem, to proﬁle its latency with the optimal intra-\\\\nop parallel plan. In AlpaServe, we keep the two compilation\\\\npasses, but extends both passes for serving.\\\\nThe inter-op pass in Alpa optimizes the overall pipeline\\\\nexecution latency, which includes the time of forward and\\\\nbackward propagation and weight synchronization. However,\\\\nin serving workloads, only forward propagation is being exe-\\\\ncuted and there is no need for weight synchronization. There-\\\\nfore, we reformulate the dynamic programming in AlpaServe\\\\nto merely focus on minimizing the maximal stage latency.\\\\nSpeciﬁcally, denote F(s,k) to be the maximum latency when\\\\nslicing layers 1 to k into s stages. We can derive F as\\\\nF(s,k) = min\\\\n1≤i≤k{max{F(s−1,i−1),latency(i,k)}},\\\\nwhere latency(i,k) denotes the latency of a stage composes\\\\nof layer i to k. In Alpa, the latency function of all possible\\\\nO(K2) combinations is being proﬁled by the intra-op pass\\\\nbecause of the complicated dependency between forward and\\\\nbackward passes. In AlpaServe, because the pipeline stages\\\\nonly perform forward propagation and only communicate\\\\nintermediate results once between layer boundaries, we can\\\\naccelerate the proﬁling by only proﬁling K layers and letting\\\\nlatency(i,k) to be the sum of the latencies for layer i to k.\\\\nThis acceleration enables us to efﬁciently enumerate different\\\\ninter- and intra-op device partition setups and generate a list\\\\nof parallel strategies for the placement algorithm in §4.2.\\\\nFor the intra-op pass, we extend the ILP in Alpa to drop\\\\nall conﬁgurations that use data parallelism. For serving work-\\\\nloads, because there is no need for weight synchronization,\\\\ndata parallelism can be achieved by the replication placement.\\\\nWe leave the decision of whether to replicate a model to the\\\\nplacement algorithm in §4.2.\\\\n4.2\\\\nPlacement Algorithm\\\\nGiven a set of models and a ﬁxed cluster, AlpaServe parti-\\\\ntions the cluster into several groups of devices. Each group\\\\nof devices selects a subset of models to serve using a shared\\\\nmodel-parallel conﬁguration. Different groups can hold the\\\\nsame model as replicas. The requests for a model are dis-\\\\npatched to the groups with the requested model replica. We\\\\ncall a speciﬁc cluster group partition, model selection, and\\\\nparallel conﬁguration as a placement. Our goal is to ﬁnd a\\\\nplacement that maximizes the SLO attainment.\\\\nHowever, ﬁnding the optimal placement is a difﬁcult combi-\\\\nnatorial optimization problem. The overall placement conﬁg-\\\\nuration space grows exponentially with the number of devices\\\\nand the number of models. To make things worse, the objec-\\\\ntive “SLO attainment” has no simple analytical formula for\\\\nan arbitrary arrival distribution. Existing tools and approxima-\\\\ntions from queueing theory can only analyze simple cases in\\\\n§3.4 and cannot model more complex situations [41]. There-\\\\nfore, we resort to a simulator-guided greedy algorithm that\\\\ncalls a simulator to compute SLO attainment.\\\\nTo compute the SLO attainment with a given set of requests\\\\nand placement, in AlpaServe, we assume we know the arrival\\\\nprocess in advance. Although short-term burstiness is impos-\\\\nsible to predict, the arrival pattern over longer timescales (e.g.,\\\\nhours or days) is often predictable [43]. Given this predictabil-\\\\nity, AlpaServe either directly uses the history request traces\\\\nor ﬁts a distribution from the trace and resamples new traces\\\\nfrom the distribution as the input workload to the simulator\\\\nto compute the SLO attainment.\\\\nWe design a two-level placement algorithm: Given a cluster\\\\ngroup partition and a shared model-parallel conﬁguration for\\\\neach group, Algorithm 1 uses a simulator-guided greedy algo-\\\\nrithm to decide which models to select for each group. Then,\\\\nAlgorithm 2 enumerates various potential cluster partitions\\\\nand parallel conﬁgurations and compares the SLO attainment\\\\nfrom Algorithm 1 to determine the optimal placement.\\\\n7\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 8 ===\\\\nAlgorithm 1 Simulator-Guided Greedy Model Selection.\\\\nInput: Model list M, device group list G, group parallel con-\\\\nﬁgurations P, workload W, beam size k (default = 1).\\\\nOutput: The model selection best_sel.\\\\nbest_sel ←/0\\\\nbeam_sels ←{/0}\\\\nwhile true do\\\\nnew_sels ←/0\\\\nfor sel ∈beam_sels do\\\\nfor (m,(g, p)) ∈M ×(G,P) do\\\\n// Parallelize the model as in §4.1.\\\\nmparallelized ←parallelize(m,g, p)\\\\nsel′ ←sel.add_model_to_group(mparallelized,g)\\\\nif sel′ is in memory constraint then\\\\nsel′.slo_attainment ←simulate(sel′,W)\\\\nnew_sels.append(sel′)\\\\nif new_sels = /0 then\\\\nbreak\\\\nbeam_sels ←top-k_SLO_attainment(new_sels)\\\\nsel∗←pick_highest_SLO_attainment(beam_sels)\\\\nif sel∗.slo_att > best_sel.slo_att then\\\\nbest_sel ←sel∗\\\\nreturn best_sel\\\\nGiven a cluster group partition with a ﬁxed model-parallel\\\\nconﬁguration for each group, Algorithm 1 selects model repli-\\\\ncas iteratively as a beam search algorithm: At each iteration,\\\\nit enumerates all possible (model, group) pairs, parallelizes\\\\nthe model on the device group with the algorithms in §4.1,\\\\nand checks whether the model can be put on the group under\\\\nthe memory constraint. For all valid selections, it runs the\\\\nsimulator and computes SLO attainment. It then picks the\\\\ntop-k solutions and enters the next iteration. The algorithm\\\\nterminates when no more replicas can be put into any groups.\\\\nThe complexity of Algorithm 1 is O(MGRSB), where M\\\\nis the number of models, G is the number of groups, R is\\\\nthe number of replicas we can put according to the memory\\\\nconstraint, S is the number of requests in the workload (the\\\\nsimulation time is proportional to the number of the requests)\\\\nand B is the beam size. It runs reasonably fast for our medium-\\\\nscale cluster when the number of requests is small. When the\\\\nnumber of requests is very large, we propose another heuristic\\\\nto accelerate: Instead of using the simulator to evaluate all\\\\n(model, group) pairs at each iteration, we can run the simu-\\\\nlator only once and place a model with the most unserved\\\\nrequests in an available group with the lowest utilization. This\\\\nreduces the time complexity to O((M +G)RS). We ﬁnd this\\\\nheuristic gives solutions with SLO attainment higher than\\\\n98% of the SLO attainment get by the original algorithm in\\\\nour benchmarks.\\\\nAlgorithm 2 enumerates different group partitions and\\\\nmodel-parallel conﬁgurations and picks the best one via mul-\\\\nAlgorithm 2 Enumeration-Based Group Partition and Model-\\\\nParallel Conﬁguration Selection.\\\\nInput: Model list M, cluster C, workload W.\\\\nOutput: The placement best_plm.\\\\nbest_plm ←/0\\\\nB ←get_potential_model_buckets(M)\\\\nfor (B1,B2,...,Bk) ∈B do\\\\nH ←get_potential_device_buckets(C,B,k)\\\\nfor (H1,H2,...,Hk) ∈H do\\\\n// Get the placement for each bucket individually.\\\\nfor i from 1 to k do\\\\nplm∗\\\\ni ←/0\\\\nG ←get_potential_group_partitions(Hi)\\\\nfor G ∈G do\\\\nP ←get_potential_parallel_conﬁgs(G)\\\\nfor P ∈P do\\\\nplm ←greedy_selection(Bi,G,P,W)\\\\nif plm.slo_att > plm∗\\\\ni .slo_att then\\\\nplm∗\\\\ni ←plm\\\\nplm∗←concat(plm∗\\\\n1,...,plm∗\\\\nk)\\\\nif plm∗.slo_att > best_plm.slo_att then\\\\nbest_plm ←plm∗\\\\nreturn best_plm\\\\ntiple calls to Algorithm 1. When designing Algorithm 2,\\\\nthe ﬁrst phenomenon we notice is that putting small and\\\\nlarge models in the same group causes convoy effects, where\\\\nthe requests of small models have to wait for the requests\\\\nof large models and miss the SLO. Therefore, in Algo-\\\\nrithm 2, we ﬁrst cluster models into model buckets. Each\\\\nbucket contains a set of models with relatively similar sizes\\\\nand every model is assigned to one and only one bucket.\\\\nSpeciﬁcally, the function get_potential_model_buckets\\\\nreturns all the possible model bucket partitions that sepa-\\\\nrate models whose latency difference is larger than a thresh-\\\\nold into different disjoint buckets. We then enumerate all\\\\nthe potential ways to assign the devices to each bucket in\\\\nget_potential_device_buckets.\\\\nBecause different buckets include a disjoint set of models,\\\\nwe can then ﬁgure out the optimal placement for each bucket\\\\nindividually. For each bucket, we enumerate possible ways\\\\nto partition the devices in the bucket into several groups in\\\\nget_potential_group_partitions and enumerate the po-\\\\ntential parallel conﬁgurations for each group with the method\\\\nin get_potential_parallel_configs. We then call Al-\\\\ngorithm 1 with greedy_placement to place models in the\\\\nmodel bucket to the groups in the device bucket. We send the\\\\nwhole workload W to Algorithm 1, which ignores the requests\\\\nthat hit the models outside of the current bucket. Finally, a\\\\ncomplete solution is got by concatenating the solutions for\\\\nall buckets. The algorithm returns the best solution it ﬁnds\\\\nduring the enumerative search process.\\\\n8\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 9 ===\\\\nEnumerating all possible choices can be slow, so we use\\\\nthe following heuristics to prune the search space. Intuitively,\\\\nwe want the different buckets to serve a similar number of\\\\nrequests per second. Therefore, we eliminate the bucket con-\\\\nﬁgurations with high discrepancies in the estimated num-\\\\nber of requests it can serve per second for each bucket.\\\\nAdditionally, in get_potential_group_partitions and\\\\nget_potential_parallel_configs, we assume all groups\\\\nhave the same size and the same parallel conﬁgurations except\\\\nfor the last group which is used when the number of devices\\\\nis not divisible by the group size.\\\\n4.3\\\\nRuntime Scheduling\\\\nWe use a simple policy to dispatch and schedule the requests at\\\\nruntime. All requests are sent to a centralized controller. The\\\\ncontroller dispatches each request to the group with the short-\\\\nest queue length. Each group manages a ﬁrst-come-ﬁrst-serve\\\\nqueue. When a group receives a request, it checks whether\\\\nit can serve the request under SLO and rejects the request if\\\\nit cannot. This is possible because the execution time of a\\\\nDNN model is very predictable and can be got in advance by\\\\nproﬁling [17]. In most of our experiments, we do not include\\\\nadvanced runtime policies such as batching [17], swapping,\\\\nand preemption [18]. These techniques are complementary to\\\\nmodel parallelism. Nevertheless, we discuss how they ﬁt into\\\\nour system.\\\\nBatching. Batching multiple requests of the same model to-\\\\ngether can increase the GPU utilization and thus increase the\\\\nthroughput of a serving system. In our system, we do ﬁnd\\\\nbatching is helpful, but the gain is limited. This is because we\\\\nmainly target large models and a small batch size can already\\\\nfully saturate the GPU, which is veriﬁed in §6.5. To isolate\\\\nthe beneﬁts of model parallelism and make the results more\\\\nexplainable, we decide to disable any batching in this paper\\\\nexcept for the experiments in §6.5.\\\\nPreemption. The optimal scheduling decision often depends\\\\non future arrivals, and leveraging preemption can help cor-\\\\nrect previous suboptimal decisions. The ﬁrst-come-ﬁrst-serve\\\\npolicy may result in convoy effects when models with signiﬁ-\\\\ncantly different execution times are placed in the same group.\\\\nWe anticipate a least-slack-time-ﬁrst policy with preemption\\\\ncan alleviate the problems [10].\\\\nSwapping. The loading overheads from the CPU or Disk to\\\\nGPU memory are signiﬁcant for large models, which is the\\\\ntarget of this paper, so we do not implement swapping in Al-\\\\npaServe. We assume all models are placed on the GPUs. This\\\\nis often required due to tight SLOs and high rates, especially\\\\nfor large models. The placement of models in AlpaServe can\\\\nbe updated in the periodic re-placement (e.g., every 24 hours).\\\\nFault tolerance. While the current design of AlpaServe does\\\\nnot have fault tolerance as a focus, we acknowledge several\\\\npotential new challenges for fault tolerance: With model par-\\\\nallelism, the failure of a single GPU could cause the entire\\\\ngroup to malfunction. Additionally, the use of a centralized\\\\ncontroller presents a single point of failure.\\\\n5\\\\nImplementation\\\\nWe implement a real system and a simulator for AlpaServe\\\\nwith about 4k lines of code in Python. The real system is\\\\nimplemented on top of an existing model-parallel training sys-\\\\ntem, Alpa [48]. We extend its auto-parallelization algorithms\\\\nfor inference settings to get the model-parallel strategies. We\\\\nthen launch an Alpa runtime for each group and dispatch\\\\nrequests to these groups via a centralized controller.\\\\nThe simulator is a continuous-time, discrete-event simula-\\\\ntor [35]. The simulator maintains a global clock and simulates\\\\nall requests and model executions on the cluster. Because the\\\\nsimulator only models discrete events, it is orders of mag-\\\\nnitude faster than the real experiments. The ﬁdelity of the\\\\nsimulator is very high because of the predictability of DNN\\\\nmodel execution, which is veriﬁed in §6.1.\\\\n6\\\\nEvaluation\\\\nIn this section, we evaluate AlpaServe’s serving ability under\\\\na variety of model and workload conditions. The evaluation is\\\\nconducted on a range of model sizes, including those that do\\\\nand do not ﬁt into a single GPU, and we show that AlpaServe\\\\nconsistently outperforms strong baselines across all model\\\\nsizes. In addition, we evaluate the robustness of AlpaServe\\\\nagainst changing arrival patterns and do ablation studies of our\\\\nproposed techniques. Evaluation results show that AlpaServe\\\\ncan greatly improve various performance metrics. Speciﬁcally,\\\\nAlpaServe can choose to save up to 2.3× devices, handle 10×\\\\nhigher rates, 6× more burstiness, or 2.5× more stringent SLO,\\\\nwhile meeting the latency SLOs for over 99% requests.\\\\n6.1\\\\nExperiment Setup\\\\nCluster testbed. The error is less than 2% in all\\\\ncases, verifying the accuracy of our simulator. Additionally,\\\\nwe conduct experiments on cluster testbed for results in §6.3.\\\\n6.2\\\\nEnd-to-end Results with Real Workloads\\\\nIn this section, we compare AlpaServe against baseline meth-\\\\nods on publicly available real traces.\\\\nWorkloads. We use two real traces: Microsoft Azure func-\\\\ntion trace 2019 (MAF1) [37] and 2021 (MAF2) [47]. They\\\\nwere originally collected from Azure serverless function in-\\\\nvocations in two weeks, and have been repurposed for ML\\\\nserving research [2,21]. The two traces exhibit distinct trafﬁc\\\\npatterns. In MAF1, each function receives steady and dense\\\\nincoming requests with gradually changing rates; in MAF2,\\\\nthe trafﬁc is very bursty and is distributed across functions\\\\nin a highly skewed way – some function receives orders of\\\\nmagnitude more requests than others. Note that most previous\\\\nworks [17] are evaluated on MAF1 only. Since there are more\\\\nfunctions than models, following previous work [2,21], given\\\\na model set from Tab. 1, we round-robin functions to models\\\\nto generate trafﬁc for each model.\\\\nSetup. SLO attainment depends on many factors. For each\\\\nmetric (1) - (4) mentioned in §6.1, we set a default value, e.g.,\\\\nthe default SLO is set as tight as 5× inference latency (SLO\\\\nScale=5). This forms a default setting, given which, we then\\\\nvary one variable (while ﬁxing others) at a time and observe\\\\nhow it affects the resulting SLO attainment. To change the\\\\ntwo variables (3) and (4), which characterize trafﬁc patterns,\\\\nwe follow Clockwork [17] and Inferline [6] and slice the\\\\noriginal traces into time windows, and ﬁt the arrivals in each\\\\ntime window with a Gamma Process parameterized by rate\\\\nand coefﬁcient of variance (CV). By scaling the rate and CV\\\\nand resampling from the processes, we can control the rate\\\\nand burstiness, respectively.\\\\nBaselines. We compare AlpaServe to two baseline methods:\\\\n(1) Selective Replication (SR): use AlpaServe’s placement al-\\\\ngorithm without model parallelism, which mimics the policy\\\\nof a wide range of existing serving systems [7,39]; (2) Clock-\\\\nwork++: an improved version of the state-of-the-art model\\\\nserving system Clockwork [17]. The original Clockwork con-\\\\ntinuously swaps models into and out of GPUs. This helps for\\\\nvery small models (e.g., w/ several million parameters) but\\\\nincurs signiﬁcant swapping overheads on larger models. For\\\\nfair comparisons, we implement Clockwork++ in our simula-\\\\ntor, which swaps models following Clockwork’s replacement\\\\nstrategy at the boundary of every two windows3 of the trace\\\\nusing SR’s algorithm, but assuming zero swapping overheads.\\\\nWe believe it represents a hypothetical upper bound of Clock-\\\\nwork’s performance. Since all the baselines can only support\\\\nmodels that can ﬁt into one GPU memory,4 we use model set\\\\nS1, S2 and S3 from Tab. 1 in this experiment.\\\\nSLO attainment vs. cluster size. Fig. 12’s ﬁrst row shows\\\\nthe SLO attainment with varying cluster sizes when serving\\\\na speciﬁc (model set, trace) pair. AlpaServe outperforms the\\\\ntwo baselines at all times and uses far fewer devices to achieve\\\\n99% SLO attainment thanks to model parallelism. Surprisingly, although we let Clockwork++ adjust\\\\nto the trafﬁc dynamically with zero overhead, AlpaServe still\\\\nwins with a static placement; this is because model-parallel\\\\nplacement is by nature more robust to bursty trafﬁc.\\\\nIt is worth noting that replication-only methods can at most\\\\nplace 2 replicas of BERT-2.6B on a V100 (13GB memory bud-\\\\nget), resulting in a substantial memory fraction, while model\\\\nparallelism can avoid such memory fractions and enable more\\\\nﬂexible placement of models.\\\\nSLO attainment vs. rate. Fig. 12’s 2nd row varies the rate of\\\\nthe workloads. For a stable trace like MAF1, AlpaServe can\\\\nhandle a much higher rate than baselines. While for a skewed\\\\nand highly dynamic trace MAF2, whose trafﬁc is dominated\\\\nby a few models and changes rapidly, the replication-based\\\\nmethods have to allocate the majority of the GPUs to create\\\\nmany replicas for “hot” models to combat their bursty trafﬁc;\\\\nthose GPUs, however, may go idle between bursts, even with\\\\nfrequent re-placement as in Clockwork++. In AlpaServe, each\\\\nmodel needs fewer replicas to handle its peak trafﬁc.\\\\nSLO attainment vs. CV. Fig. 12’s 3rd row varies the CV of\\\\nthe workloads. The trafﬁc becomes more bursty with a higher\\\\nCV, which aggravates the queuing effect of the system and\\\\nincreases the possibility of SLO violation. The traditional\\\\nsolution to handle burstiness is by over-provision, wasting a\\\\nlot of resources. AlpaServe reveals a hidden opportunity to\\\\nhandle this by model parallelism.\\\\nSLO attainment vs. SLO. Fig. 12’s 4th row shows the effect\\\\nof different SLO. Previous work [17] which targets serving\\\\nsmall models usually sets SLO to hundreds of milliseconds,\\\\neven though the actual inference latency is less than 10 ms.\\\\nThanks to the intra-op parallelism, AlpaServe can maintain\\\\ngood performance under similar SLO when serving large\\\\nmodels, whose inference latency can be over 100 ms. When\\\\nSLO is tight, even less than the model inference time, Al-\\\\npaServe favors intra-op parallelism to reduce the inference\\\\nlatency, which also reduces AlpaServe’s peak throughput due\\\\nto the communication overhead but can make more requests\\\\nto meet their SLO. When SLO becomes looser, AlpaServe\\\\nwill automatically switch to use more inter-op parallelism to\\\\nget higher throughput.\\\\n6.3\\\\nServing Very Large Models\\\\nToday’s large models may possess hundreds of billions of\\\\nparameters [3, 27, 46]. To serve large models at this scale,\\\\nthe common practice in production is to choose the model\\\\nparallelism strategy manually and use dedicated GPUs for\\\\neach model [45]. To show AlpaServe has improved capability\\\\nin serving very large models, we deploy model set S4 on our\\\\ntestbed, each requiring at least 16 GPUs to serve in terms of\\\\n11\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 12 ===\\\\n2.5\\\\n5.0\\\\n7.5\\\\nRate (r/s)\\\\n60\\\\n70\\\\n80\\\\n90\\\\n100\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n3\\\\n4\\\\nCV\\\\n60\\\\n70\\\\n80\\\\n90\\\\n100\\\\n2.5\\\\n5.0\\\\n7.5\\\\nSLO Scale\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\nSLO Attainment (%)\\\\nAlpaServe\\\\n(16,1)\\\\n(8,2)\\\\n(4,4)\\\\n(2,8)\\\\nFigure 13: SLO attainment as we vary the rate, CV, and SLO\\\\nscale. We check\\\\nthe solution of AlpaServe and ﬁnd it slices the cluster evenly\\\\ninto two groups, each with the (4, 8) inter-/intra-op parallel\\\\nconﬁguration, and groups the models in a way that balances\\\\nthe requests between two groups. By\\\\nspace-sharing the devices, AlpaServe can exploit new oppor-\\\\ntunities for statistical multiplexing, which is advantageous for\\\\nbursty workloads but largely under-explored by prior work.\\\\n6.4\\\\nRobustness to Changing Trafﬁc Patterns\\\\nUntil now, AlpaServe’s good performance is based on the\\\\nassumption we make in its placement algorithm that we know\\\\nthe arrival process in advance. In practice, the arrival process\\\\ncan be approximated using historical traces but the unavoid-\\\\nable real-world variance may make the prediction inaccurate.\\\\nIn this experiment, we study how AlpaServe performs if the\\\\ntrafﬁc patterns change.\\\\nWe reuse the same setting for S2@MAF1 in §6.2, but this\\\\ntime for AlpaServe and SR, we randomly slice two one-hour\\\\ntraces from MAF1, one is what their algorithms are assumed,\\\\nwhile the other one is used as the actual arrival process. While\\\\n5Uniform split yielded similar results.\\\\nfor Clockwork++, we still run its algorithm directly on the\\\\nactual arrival process to respect its online nature. Similarly,\\\\nwe vary different factors and compute the SLO attainment for\\\\neach system. We repeat the experiments three times and show\\\\nthe average results in Fig. 14.\\\\nUnsurprisingly, SR’s performance drops signiﬁcantly when\\\\ntrafﬁc changes. By contrast, AlpaServe maintains good per-\\\\nformance and still outperforms Clockwork++, an online ad-\\\\njustment algorithm, using a static placement generated from\\\\nsubstantially different trafﬁc patterns. This conﬁrms that, in\\\\nface of highly-dynamic trafﬁc patterns, statistical multiplex-\\\\ning with model parallelism is a simple and better alternative\\\\nthan existing replication- or replacement-based algorithms.\\\\n6.5\\\\nBeneﬁts of Dynamic Batching\\\\nBatching is a common optimization in other serving sys-\\\\ntems [17, 29, 30] and the choice of batch size is critical to\\\\nthe performance because it can increase GPU utilization and\\\\nthus increase the system throughput. However, in large model\\\\nscenarios, the beneﬁt of batching is limited mainly due to\\\\ntwo reasons. First, for large models, a small batch size will\\\\nsaturate the GPU, which means there is little gain to batching\\\\nmore requests. Second, the execution latency grows linearly\\\\nwith the batch size [39], so when the SLO is tight (say SLO\\\\nScale is less than 2), batching is simply not a choice.\\\\nTo isolate the beneﬁts of model parallelism and make the\\\\nresults more explainable, we decide to disable any batching\\\\nin other experiments but prove that the batching strategy is\\\\npurely orthogonal to the scope of this paper in this subsection.\\\\nTo prove this, we implement a standard batching algorithm in\\\\nAlpaServe and evaluate its performance.\\\\nBatching strategy. When a request arrives, it will get exe-\\\\ncuted immediately if any device group is available. Otherwise,\\\\nit will be put into a per-model requests queue for batching.\\\\nWhen a device group becomes idle, it will choose a model\\\\nwhich has a replica on it and batch as many requests as possi-\\\\nble from the requests queue of the model while satisfying the\\\\nSLO requirements.\\\\nSetup. As the model size increases, the potential beneﬁt of\\\\nbatching decreases. Therefore, we choose to evaluate model\\\\nset S1. We generate a synthetic Gamma Process trafﬁc with\\\\nan average rate of 4 requests/s and a CV of 4 for each model.\\\\nSLO attainment. Fig. 15 (left) shows the SLO attainment\\\\nachieved by AlpaServe with different maximum batch size set-\\\\ntings under various SLO scales. When the SLO requirement\\\\nis tight, any batching will violate the SLO so there is no gain\\\\nwith batching enabled. Also, although we choose to serve the\\\\nsmallest model in Tab. 1, a small batch size like 2 combined\\\\nwith a long sequence length of 2048 already saturates the\\\\nGPU, so a larger maximum batch size brings no performance\\\\nimprovement. Fig. 15 (right) compares the improvement for\\\\nAlpaServe and Clockwork++ with our batching algorithm\\\\n12\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 13 ===\\\\n10\\\\n20\\\\n30\\\\n40\\\\n50\\\\n#devices\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\n0.002\\\\n0.004\\\\n0.006\\\\n0.008\\\\nRate Scale\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n6\\\\n8\\\\nCV Scale\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n6\\\\n8\\\\n10\\\\nSLO Scale\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\nSLO Attainment (%)\\\\nAlpaServe\\\\nClockwork++\\\\nSR\\\\nFigure 14: The actual arrival trafﬁc for AlpaServe and SR is different from what their algorithms are assumed, while Clockwork++\\\\nruns directly on the actual trafﬁc.\\\\n0.0\\\\n2.5\\\\n5.0\\\\n7.5\\\\n10.0\\\\n12.5\\\\nSLO Scale\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\nAlpaServe\\\\nAlpaServe (mb=2)\\\\nAlpaServe (mb=4)\\\\nAlpaServe (mb=8)\\\\nAlpaServe (mb=16)\\\\n0.0\\\\n2.5\\\\n5.0\\\\n7.5\\\\n10.0\\\\n12.5\\\\nSLO Scale\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\nAlpaServe\\\\nClockwork++\\\\nAlpaServe (mb=2)\\\\nClockwork++ (mb=2)\\\\nSLO Attainment (%)\\\\nFigure 15: SLO Attainment when batching is enabled. mb=2\\\\nmeans the maximum batch size is 2.\\\\nenabled.6 When the SLO requirement becomes loose, both\\\\nAlpaServe and Clockwork++ have better SLO attainment to\\\\nsome extent. We show that the auto-\\\\nparallelization ability allows AlpaServe to not only gener-\\\\nalize to arbitrary model architectures but even also reduce\\\\nparallelism overheads – hence improved serving performance\\\\n(see §3.3 for more discussion). To see that, typical manual\\\\nmodel-parallel parallelization strategies offered in de facto\\\\nsystems [1, 27, 28] is to assign an equal number of (trans-\\\\nformer) layers to each pipeline stage. These strategies often\\\\nfail to create balanced workloads across distributed GPUs be-\\\\ncause contemporary large models have heterogeneous layers,\\\\nsuch as embedding operations. The extensions introduced in\\\\n§4.1 automatically partition the models at the computational\\\\ngraph level and generate nearly-balanced stages. Empirically,\\\\nas shown in Fig. 16, for 8 pipeline stages, auto-parallelization\\\\nreduces the total overhead by 32.9% and 46.7% for Trans-\\\\nformer 1.3B and 2.6B respectively, which is necessary for\\\\nachieving good serving performance when model parallelism\\\\nis used for serving.\\\\nEffectiveness of the placement algorithm. We now test the\\\\neffectiveness of our placement algorithm on a synthetic work-\\\\n6SR is left out to make the ﬁgure clearer as it is worse than Clockwork++.\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\nNumber of GPUs\\\\n0.100\\\\n0.125\\\\n0.150\\\\n0.175\\\\n0.200\\\\n0.225\\\\n0.250\\\\nLatency (s)\\\\nCompuation\\\\nCommunication Overhead\\\\nUneven Partition Overhead\\\\n(a) Transformer 1.3B.\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\nNumber of GPUs\\\\n0.20\\\\n0.22\\\\n0.24\\\\n0.26\\\\n0.28\\\\n0.30\\\\nLatency (s)\\\\nCompuation\\\\nCommunication Overhead\\\\nUneven Partition Overhead\\\\n(b) Transformer 2.6B.\\\\nFigure 16: Comparison of the model parallel overhead be-\\\\ntween manual partition (lighter color) and the partition found\\\\nby the automatic algorithm (darker color).\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\n#models\\\\n60\\\\n65\\\\n70\\\\n75\\\\n80\\\\n85\\\\n90\\\\n95\\\\n100\\\\nRound robin\\\\nGreedy placement\\\\nGreedy placement + Group partitioning\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80\\\\n100\\\\n120\\\\nRate Scale\\\\n60\\\\n65\\\\n70\\\\n75\\\\n80\\\\n85\\\\n90\\\\n95\\\\n100\\\\nRound robin\\\\nGreedy placement\\\\nGreedy placement + Group partitioning\\\\nSLO Attainment (%)\\\\nFigure 17: Ablation study of placement algorithms.\\\\nload. There has been a proliferation of\\\\nmodel serving systems recently. These range from general-\\\\n13\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 14 ===\\\\npurpose production-grade systems like TensorFlow Serv-\\\\ning [30] and NVIDIA Triton [29], which are widely used but\\\\ndo not provide any support for automatic placement or latency\\\\nconstraints. They also include systems that are optimized for\\\\nsingle-model serving [45] or serving of speciﬁc classes of\\\\nmodels (e.g., transformers) [14,45,49]. AlpaServe targets a\\\\nbroader set of models and features than these systems.\\\\nFor SLO-aware, distributed serving, most serving systems\\\\nignore placement-level interactions between models. Clock-\\\\nwork [17], for instance, primarily focuses on predictability;\\\\nwhen scheduling, it greedily loads and executes models on\\\\navailable GPUs. For large models, loading model weights\\\\ncan easily overwhelm practical SLOs. Other systems like\\\\nClipper [7] and DVABatch [8] also do not reason about the\\\\nlatencies of co-located models.\\\\nNexus [39] is very related to our work in that it exam-\\\\nines the placement of models; however, Nexus is an example\\\\nof a system that takes the traditional replication approach\\\\ndescribed in §3 and, thus, misses a broad class of potential\\\\nparallelization strategies that we explore in this paper.\\\\nInference optimizations for large models. AlpaServe is\\\\ncomplementary to another large body of work on optimiza-\\\\ntions for inference over large models. These include tech-\\\\nniques like quantization [11], distillation [36], ofﬂoading [1],\\\\nbetter operator parallelism [32], and CUDA kernel optimiza-\\\\ntion [9,22]. Some of these optimizations are intended to stem\\\\nthe tide of increasing model sizes; however, all of these gains\\\\nare partial— the challenge of serving large models has con-\\\\ntinued to escalate rapidly despite these efforts.\\\\nModel parallelism for training. AlpaServe is largely or-\\\\nthogonal to the large body of work on model parallelism in\\\\ntraining [19,27,33,48]. As described in §3, serving presents\\\\na unique set of constraints and opportunities not found in\\\\ntraining workloads. Where these systems do intersect with\\\\nAlpaServe, however, is in their methods for implementing\\\\nmodel parallelism along various dimensions. In particular,\\\\nAlpaServe builds on some of the parallelization techniques\\\\nintroduced in [48].\\\\nResource allocation and multiplexing. The problem of how\\\\nto allocate and multiplex limited resources to a set of incoming\\\\nrequests is one of the oldest topics in computer science [25,\\\\n34]. Rather, the contribution of this paper is a deep empirical\\\\nanalysis of the applications of these ideas to an emerging\\\\nspace: the serving of large models.\\\\n8\\\\nConclusion\\\\nIn this paper, we presented AlpaServe, a system for prediction\\\\nservings of multiple large deep-learning models. The key\\\\ninnovation of AlpaServe is integrating model parallelism into\\\\nmulti-model serving. Because of the inherent overheads of\\\\nmodel parallelism, such parallelism is traditionally applied\\\\nconservatively—reserved for cases where models simply do\\\\nnot ﬁt within a single GPU or execute within the required SLO.\\\\nAlpaServe demonstrates that model parallelism is useful for\\\\nmany other scenarios, quantiﬁes the tradeoffs, and presents\\\\ntechniques to automatically navigate that tradeoff space.\\\\nReferences\\\\n[1] Reza Yazdani Aminabadi, Samyam Rajbhandari, Min-\\\\njia Zhang, Ammar Ahmad Awan, Cheng Li, Du Li, El-\\\\nton Zheng, Jeff Rasley, Shaden Smith, Olatunji Ruwase,\\\\net al. Gonzalez 1 Ion Stoica 1\\\\nABSTRACT\\\\nThe “pretrain-then-finetune” paradigm is commonly adopted in the deployment of large language models. Low-\\\\nRank Adaptation (LoRA), a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, is often employed to adapt a base model to a\\\\nmultitude of tasks, resulting in a substantial collection of LoRA adapters derived from one base model. We observe\\\\nthat this paradigm presents significant opportunities for batched inference during serving. To capitalize on these\\\\nopportunities, we present S-LoRA, a system designed for the scalable serving of many LoRA adapters. S-LoRA\\\\nstores all adapters in the main memory and fetches the adapters used by the currently running queries to the\\\\nGPU memory. To efficiently use the GPU memory and reduce fragmentation, S-LoRA proposes Unified Paging.\\\\nUnified Paging uses a unified memory pool to manage dynamic adapter weights with different ranks and KV cache\\\\ntensors with varying sequence lengths. Additionally, S-LoRA employs a novel tensor parallelism strategy and\\\\nhighly optimized custom CUDA kernels for heterogeneous batching of LoRA computation. Collectively, these\\\\nfeatures enable S-LoRA to serve thousands of LoRA adapters on a single GPU or across multiple GPUs with a\\\\nsmall overhead. Compared to state-of-the-art libraries such as HuggingFace PEFT and vLLM (with naive support\\\\nof LoRA serving), S-LoRA can improve the throughput by up to 4 times and increase the number of served\\\\nadapters by several orders of magnitude. As a result, S-LoRA enables scalable serving of many task-specific\\\\nfine-tuned models and offers the potential for large-scale customized fine-tuning services.\\\\n1\\\\nINTRODUCTION\\\\nLarge language models (LLMs) have become ubiquitous in\\\\nmodern applications, ranging from natural language pro-\\\\ncessing to more general tasks (OpenAI, 2023; Touvron\\\\net al., 2023b; Alayrac et al., 2022). Within these domains,\\\\nLLMs have consistently demonstrated superior performance,\\\\nespecially when fine-tuned for specific tasks (Kenton &\\\\nToutanova, 2019; Houlsby et al., 2019; Ouyang et al., 2022).\\\\nThis “pretrain-then-finetune” paradigm has led to the pro-\\\\nliferation of numerous fine-tuned variants of a single base\\\\nLLM, each tailored to a specific task or domain.\\\\nWhen scaling the fine-tuning of a base model for numerous\\\\ntasks, such as personalized assistants, the associated train-\\\\ning and serving costs can become substantial. To address\\\\nthis, several parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods have\\\\nbeen developed. A prime exemplar is Low-Rank Adaptation\\\\n(LoRA) (Hu et al., 2021), which enables efficient fine-tuning\\\\nby updating only low-rank additive matrices. These matri-\\\\nces consist of a small number of parameters, referred to as\\\\nadapter weights. LoRA has shown that by fine-tuning just\\\\n*Equal contribution. Part of the work was done when Ying\\\\nwas visiting UC Berkeley.\\\\n1UC Berkeley 2Stanford University\\\\n3Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Correspondence to: Ying Sheng\\\\n<ying1123@stanford.edu>, Shiyi Cao <shicao@berkeley.edu>.\\\\nthese adapter weights, it is possible to achieve performance\\\\non par with full-weight fine-tuning. However, despite con-\\\\nsiderable research into fine-tuning, the question of how to\\\\nserve these fine-tuned variants at scale remains unexplored.\\\\nOne of the key innovations in the LoRA paper was the\\\\nelimination of adapter inference latency by directly merging\\\\nthe adapter with the model parameters. Additionally, to\\\\nsupport multiple models on a single machine, the same\\\\npaper proposes swapping adapters by adding and subtracting\\\\nLoRA weights from the base model. While this approach\\\\nenables low-latency inference for a single adapter and serial\\\\nexecution across adapters, it significantly reduces overall\\\\nserving throughput and increases total latency when serving\\\\nmultiple adapters concurrently. Moreover, the paper does\\\\nnot consider the opportunity to leverage host memory to\\\\nincrease the number of adapters hosted by a single machine.\\\\nIn this paper, we study how to scalably serve thousands\\\\nof LoRA adapters on a single machine. We observe that\\\\nthe shared base model, which underpins numerous LoRA\\\\nadapters, presents a substantial opportunity for batched in-\\\\nference. To achieve high-throughput multi-adapter serving,\\\\nit is advantageous to separate the batchable base model\\\\ncomputation from individual LoRA computations.\\\\nWhile leveraging batching in the base model is straight-\\\\nforward (as all queries share the base model), extending\\\\narXiv:2311.03285v1  [cs.LG]  6 Nov 2023\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 2 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\nbatching to the adapters is challenging. First, serving many\\\\nLoRA adapters simultaneously requires efficient memory\\\\nmanagement. Since GPU memory is limited, we must store\\\\nadapter weights outside the GPU and dynamically fetch\\\\nthem when needed. However, dynamically loading and un-\\\\nloading adapters of varying sizes, coupled with the dynamic\\\\nallocation and deallocation of KV cache tensors for requests\\\\nwith different sequence lengths, can lead to significant mem-\\\\nory fragmentation and I/O overhead. Second, apart from\\\\nthe easily batchable base model computation, the separated\\\\ncomputation of many adapters with distinct ranks in non-\\\\ncontiguous memory is challenging to batch and demands the\\\\ndevelopment of new computation kernels. Third, leveraging\\\\nmultiple GPUs on a single machine requires novel paral-\\\\nlelism strategies to accommodate the added LoRA weights\\\\nand computations. It is essential to carefully design this strat-\\\\negy to minimize communication and memory overheads.\\\\nTo this end, we introduce S-LoRA, a scalable LoRA serving\\\\nsystem. S-LoRA exploits batching opportunities, efficiently\\\\nmanages both host and GPU memory, and orchestrates par-\\\\nallelism across multiple GPUs. The primary contributions\\\\nof S-LoRA are summarized as follows:\\\\n• Unified Paging: To reduce memory fragmentation and\\\\nincrease batch size, S-LoRA introduces a unified mem-\\\\nory pool. This pool manages dynamic adapter weights\\\\nand KV cache tensors by a unified paging mechanism.\\\\n• Heterogeneous Batching: To minimize the latency over-\\\\nhead when batching different adapters of varying ranks,\\\\nS-LoRA employs highly optimized custom CUDA ker-\\\\nnels. These kernels operate directly on non-contiguous\\\\nmemory and align with the memory pool design, fa-\\\\ncilitating efficient batched inference for added LoRA\\\\ncomputation.\\\\n• S-LoRA TP: To ensure effective parallelization across\\\\nmultiple GPUs, S-LoRA introduces a novel tensor par-\\\\nallelism strategy. This approach incurs minimal com-\\\\nmunication cost for the added LoRA computation com-\\\\npared to that of the base model. This is realized by\\\\nscheduling communications on small intermediate ten-\\\\nsors and fusing them with the communications of the\\\\nbase model.\\\\nWe evaluate S-LoRA by serving Llama-7B/13B/30B/70B.\\\\nResults show that S-LoRA can serve thousands of LoRA\\\\nadapters on a single GPU or across multiple GPUs with\\\\na small overhead. When compared to the state-of-the-art\\\\nparameter-efficient fine-tuning library, Huggingface PEFT,\\\\nS-LoRA can enhance throughput by up to 30×. In com-\\\\nparison to the high-throughput serving system vLLM using\\\\na naive support of LoRA serving, S-LoRA can improve\\\\nthroughput by up to 4× and increase the number of served\\\\nadapters by several orders of magnitude. The code is avail-\\\\nable at https://github.com/S-LoRA/S-LoRA.\\\\n2\\\\nBACKGROUND\\\\nLow-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2021) is a\\\\nparameter-efficient fine-tuning method designed to adapt\\\\npre-trained large language models to new tasks. The mo-\\\\ntivation behind LoRA stems from the low intrinsic dimen-\\\\nsionality of model updates during adaptation. In the training\\\\nphase, LoRA freezes the weights of a pre-trained base model\\\\nand adds trainable low-rank matrices to each layer. This\\\\napproach significantly reduces the number of trainable pa-\\\\nrameters and memory consumption. When compared to full\\\\nparameter fine-tuning, LoRA can often reduce the number of\\\\ntrainable parameters by orders of magnitude (e.g., 10000×)\\\\nwhile retaining comparable accuracy. For the inference\\\\nphase, the original paper suggests merging the low-rank\\\\nmatrices with the weights of the base model. As a result,\\\\nthere is no added overhead during inference, setting it apart\\\\nfrom previous adapters like (Houlsby et al., 2019) or prompt\\\\ntuning methods such as (Lester et al., 2021).\\\\nFormally, for a pre-trained weight matrix W ∈Rh×d, LoRA\\\\nintroduces the update as W ′ = W +AB, where A ∈Rh×r,\\\\nB ∈Rr×d, and the rank r ≪min(h, d). If the forward pass\\\\nof a base model is defined by h = xW, then after applying\\\\nLoRA, the forward pass becomes\\\\nh = xW ′ = x(W + AB)\\\\n(1)\\\\n= xW + xAB.\\\\n(2)\\\\nTypically, this adjustment is only applied to the query, key,\\\\nvalue, and output projection matrices in the self-attention\\\\nmodule, excluding the feed-forward module.\\\\nBecause LoRA greatly reduces the training and weight stor-\\\\nage costs, it has been widely adopted by the community,\\\\nand people have created hundreds of thousands of LoRA\\\\nadapters for pre-trained large language models and diffusion\\\\nmodels (Mangrulkar et al., 2022).\\\\n2.1\\\\nServing Large Language Models\\\\nMost large language models (LLMs) are based on the trans-\\\\nformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017). The number of\\\\nparameters in an LLM ranges from several billion to several\\\\ntrillion (Brown et al., 2020; Chowdhery et al., 2022; Fedus\\\\net al., 2022), corresponding to disk sizes spanning several gi-\\\\ngabytes to even terabytes. This scale results in LLM serving\\\\nhaving significant computational and memory demands.\\\\nAdditionally, the inference process for LLMs requires iter-\\\\native autoregressive decoding. Initially, the model carries\\\\nout a forward pass to encode the prompt. Following this, it\\\\ndecodes the output one token at a time. The sequential pro-\\\\ncess makes decoding slow. Since each token attends to the\\\\nhidden states of all its preceding tokens, it becomes essential\\\\nto store the hidden states of all previous tokens. This storage\\\\nis referred to as the “KV cache”. Such a mechanism adds to\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 3 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\nthe memory overhead and causes the decoding process to\\\\nbe more memory-intensive than computation-intensive.\\\\nThe challenges become even more pronounced in online\\\\nsettings, where requests of varying sequence lengths ar-\\\\nrive dynamically. To accommodate such dynamic incoming\\\\nrequests, Orca (Yu et al., 2022) introduces a method of fine-\\\\ngrained, iteration-level scheduling. Instead of scheduling at\\\\nthe request level, Orca batches at the token level. This ap-\\\\nproach allows for the continuous addition of new requests to\\\\nthe currently running batch, resulting in substantially higher\\\\nthroughput. vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) further optimizes\\\\nOrca’s memory efficiency using PagedAttention. PagedAt-\\\\ntention adopts concepts from virtual memory and paging in\\\\noperating systems and manages the storage and access of\\\\ndynamic KV cache tensors in a paged fashion. This method\\\\nefficiently reduces fragmentation, facilitating larger batch\\\\nsizes and higher throughput.\\\\nWhen serving very large models that exceed the memory\\\\ncapacity of a single GPU, or when there are stringent la-\\\\ntency requirements, it is necessary to parallelize the model\\\\nacross multiple GPUs. Several model parallelism methods\\\\nhave been proposed, such as tensor parallelism (Shoeybi\\\\net al., 2019), sequence parallelism (Korthikanti et al., 2023),\\\\npipeline parallelism (Huang et al., 2019), and their combi-\\\\nnations (Narayanan et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2022).\\\\n3\\\\nOVERVIEW OF S-LORA\\\\nS-LoRA encompasses three principal components of in-\\\\nnovation. In Section 4, we introduce our batching strat-\\\\negy, which decomposes the computation between the base\\\\nmodel and the LoRA adapters. Additionally, we address\\\\nthe challenge of request scheduling, covering aspects like\\\\nadapter clustering and admission control. The ability to\\\\nbatch across concurrent adapters, introduces new challenges\\\\naround memory management. In Section 5, we generalize\\\\nPagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023) to Unfied Paging which\\\\nsupport dynamically loading LoRA adapters. This approach\\\\nuses a unified memory pool to store the KV caches and\\\\nadapter weights in a paged fashion, which can reduce frag-\\\\nmentation and balance the dynamic changing size of the\\\\nKV caches and adapter weights. Lastly, in Section 6, we\\\\nintroduce our new tensor parallelism strategy that enables us\\\\nto efficiently decoupled the base model and LoRA adapters.\\\\n4\\\\nBATCHING AND SCHEDULING\\\\n4.1\\\\nBatching\\\\nOur batching strategy aims to support online and high-\\\\nthroughput serving of many LoRA adapters simultaneously.\\\\nFor a single adapter, the method recommended by (Hu et al.,\\\\n2021) is to merge the adapter weights into the base model\\\\nW\\\\nx1\\\\nx2\\\\nx3\\\\nx\\\\nA\\\\n1\\\\nB1\\\\nx1\\\\nx\\\\nx\\\\nx2\\\\nA\\\\n2\\\\nB2\\\\nx\\\\nx\\\\nx3\\\\nA\\\\n3\\\\nB3\\\\nx\\\\nx\\\\nx\\\\nBatched base computation\\\\nBatched LoRA computation\\\\nadd\\\\nFigure 1. Separated batched computation for the base model and\\\\nLoRA computation. The batched computation of the base model\\\\nis implemented by GEMM. The batched computation for LoRA\\\\nadapters is implemented by custom CUDA kernels which support\\\\nbatching various sequence lengths and adapter ranks.\\\\nMain Memory\\\\nAdapter 1\\\\nAdapter 2\\\\nAdapter 3\\\\nAdapter 4\\\\nAdapter 5\\\\nAdapter 6\\\\n…\\\\nGPU Memory\\\\nKV cache\\\\nUnified memory pool\\\\nfor dynamic tensors\\\\nBase\\\\nModel\\\\nWeights\\\\nOther\\\\nTemporary\\\\nTensors\\\\nFetch active \\\\nadapters for\\\\nthe current batch\\\\nAdapter 2\\\\nAdapter 5\\\\nFigure 2. Overview of memory allocation in S-LoRA. S-LoRA\\\\nstores all adapters in the main memory and fetches the active\\\\nadapters for the current batch to the GPU memory. The GPU\\\\nmemory is used to store the KV cache, adapter weights, base\\\\nmodel weights, and other temporary tensors.\\\\nweights, resulting in a new model (see Eq. 1). This has the\\\\nadvantage that there is no additional adapter overhead during\\\\ninference, since the new model has the same number of\\\\nparameters as the base model. In fact, this was a prominent\\\\nfeature of the original LoRA work.\\\\nHowever, when there are multiple adapters, merging the\\\\nweights into the base model leads to multiple weight copies\\\\nand missed batching opportunities. Directly merging the\\\\nmodels requires maintaining many copies of the full lan-\\\\nguage model. In the original LoRA paper, the authors pro-\\\\nposed adding and subtracting LoRA weights on the fly to\\\\nenable serving multiple models without increasing the mem-\\\\nory overhead. However, this approach doesn’t support con-\\\\ncurrent inference on separate LoRA adapters and therefore\\\\nlimits batching opportunities.\\\\nIn this paper, we show that merging LoRA adapters into\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 4 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\nthe base model is inefficient for the multi-LoRA high-\\\\nthroughput serving setting. Instead, we propose computing\\\\nthe LoRA computation xAB on-the-fly as shown in Eq. 2.\\\\nThis avoids weight duplication and enables batching of the\\\\nmore costly xW operation. But this approach also increases\\\\nthe computation overhead. However, because the cost of\\\\nxAB is substantially lower than xW and there is a consid-\\\\nerable savings from batching xW across different adapters,\\\\nwe show that the savings far exceed the additional overhead.\\\\nUnfortunately, directly implementing the factored computa-\\\\ntion of the base model and individual LoRA adapters using\\\\nthe batch GEMM kernel from the existing BLAS libraries\\\\nwould require significant padding and result in poor hard-\\\\nware utilization. This is because of the heterogeneity of\\\\nsequence lengths and adapter ranks.\\\\nIn S-LoRA, we batch the computation of the base model and\\\\nthen employ custom CUDA kernels to execute the additional\\\\nxAB for all adapters separately. This process is illustrated\\\\nby Figure 1. Instead of naively using padding and using the\\\\nbatch GEMM kernel from the BLAS library for the LoRA\\\\ncomputation, we implement custom CUDA kernels for more\\\\nefficient computation without padding. In Subsection 5.3,\\\\nwe discuss the implementation details.\\\\nWhile the number of LoRA adapters can be large if we\\\\nstore them in main memory, the number of LoRA adapters\\\\nneeded for the currently running batch is manageable, be-\\\\ncause the batch size is bounded by the GPU memory. To\\\\ntake advantage of this, we store all LoRA adapters in the\\\\nmain memory and fetch only the LoRA adapters needed\\\\nfor the currently running batch to the GPU RAM when\\\\nrunning the inference for that batch. In this case, the max-\\\\nimum number of adapters that can be served is bounded\\\\nby the main memory size. This process is illustrated by\\\\nFigure 2. To achieve high-throughput serving, we adopt the\\\\niteration-level scheduling batching strategy from Orca (Yu\\\\net al., 2022). In this approach, requests are scheduled at the\\\\ntoken level. We immediately incorporate a new request into\\\\nthe running batch if space is available. The request will exit\\\\nthe batch once it reaches the maximum number of gener-\\\\nated tokens or fulfills other stopping criteria. This process\\\\nreduces GPU memory usage but introduces new memory\\\\nmanagement challenges. In Section 5, we will discuss our\\\\ntechniques to manage memory efficiently.\\\\n4.2\\\\nAdapter Clustering\\\\nTo enhance batching efficiency, one potential strategy is\\\\nreducing the number of active adapters in a running batch.\\\\nBy using fewer adapters, there is an opportunity to allocate\\\\nmore memory to the KV cache, which in turn can facili-\\\\ntate larger batch sizes. Given the common memory capaci-\\\\nties of GPUs, they are often underutilized while decoding.\\\\nConsequently, increasing the batch size can lead to higher\\\\nthroughput. A direct approach to reducing the number of\\\\nadapters in a running batch is to prioritize batching requests\\\\nthat use the same adapter, a strategy we term “adapter clus-\\\\ntering”. However, adapter clustering comes with its own set\\\\nof trade-offs. For example, it can hurt the average latency\\\\nor fairness among adapters. We provide an ablation study in\\\\nAppendix A to illustrate how throughput and latency change\\\\naccording to the cluster size.\\\\n4.3\\\\nAdmission Control\\\\nIn S-LoRA, we also applied an admission control strategy\\\\nto sustain good attainment when the traffic is higher than the\\\\nserving system capacity. A serving system is typically char-\\\\nacterized by a service level objective (SLO) which specifies\\\\nthe desired latency of processing requests. If the serving\\\\nsystem has fixed capacity, it must implement an admission\\\\ncontrol mechanism, that drops a request, if the system can-\\\\nnot meet its SLO. Otherwise, if no request is dropped, and\\\\nthe number of incoming requests is larger than the system\\\\ncapacity for long enough, the serving system is bound to\\\\nviolate the SLO. We implemented an abort strategy to mimic\\\\nadmission control in S-LoRA, called early abort strategy.\\\\nIntuitively, we estimate the set of latest requests that we\\\\ncan serve in SLO, and then serve them in the order of ar-\\\\nrival time. More implementation details and mathematical\\\\njustifications are deferred to Appendix B.\\\\n5\\\\nMEMORY MANAGEMENT\\\\nCompared to serving a single base model, serving multiple\\\\nLoRA adapters simultaneously presents new memory man-\\\\nagement challenges. To support many adapters, S-LoRA\\\\nstores them in the main memory and dynamically loads the\\\\nadapter weights needed for the currently running batch into\\\\nGPU RAM. During this process, there are two noticeable\\\\nchallenges. The first is memory fragmentation, resulting\\\\nfrom the dynamic loading and offloading adapter weights of\\\\nvarious sizes. The second is the latency overhead introduced\\\\nby adapter loading and offloading. To tackle these chal-\\\\nlenges efficiently, we propose Unfied Paging and overlap\\\\nthe I/O with computation by prefetching adapter weights.\\\\n5.1\\\\nUnified Paging\\\\nUnderstanding the nature of adapter weights is essential for\\\\noptimizing memory usage. Our primary observation is that\\\\nthese dynamic adapter weights are analogous to dynamic\\\\nKV caches in several ways:\\\\n• Variable sizes and operations: Just as the size of\\\\nKV cache size fluctuates with the sequence length, the\\\\nranks of the active adapters can also depend on the\\\\nchoice of adapter associated with each request. KV\\\\ncaches are allocated when requests arrive and deal-\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 5 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\nKV caches\\\\nAdapter weights\\\\nEmpty\\\\nH\\\\nFigure 3. Unified memory pool. We use a unified memory pool to\\\\nstore both KV caches and adapter weights in a non-contiguous way\\\\nto reduce memory fragmentation. The page size is H elements.\\\\nlocated once the requests are completed. Similarly,\\\\nadapter weights are loaded and cleared with each re-\\\\nquest. If not managed properly, this variability can\\\\nresult in fragmentation.\\\\n• Dimensionality: A KV cache tensor for a request in\\\\na layer has a shape of (S, H), where S denotes the se-\\\\nquence length and H represents the hidden dimension.\\\\nMeanwhile, the shape of a LoRA weight is (R, H),\\\\nwith R standing for the rank and H the hidden dimen-\\\\nsion. Both share a dimension size of H that can be\\\\nleveraged to reduce fragmentation.\\\\nMotivated by these parallels, we extend the idea of Page-\\\\ndAttention (Kwon et al., 2023) to Unified Paging which\\\\nmanages adapter weights in addition to the KV cache. Uni-\\\\nfied Paging uses a unified memory pool to jointly manage\\\\nboth KV cache and adapter weights. To implement this, we\\\\nfirst allocate a large buffer statically for the memory pool.\\\\nThis buffer uses all available space except for the space oc-\\\\ncupied by the base model weights and temporary activation\\\\ntensors. Both KV caches and adapter weights are stored in\\\\nthis memory pool in a paged manner, with each page corre-\\\\nsponding to a vector of H. Thus, a KV cache tensor with a\\\\nsequence length of S uses up S pages, while a LoRA weight\\\\ntensor of rank R takes up R pages. Figure 3 illustrates the\\\\nlayout of our memory pool, where KV caches and adapter\\\\nweights are stored interleaved and non-contiguously. This\\\\napproach significantly reduces fragmentation, ensuring that\\\\nadapters weights of various ranks can coexist with dynamic\\\\nKV caches in a structured and systematic manner.\\\\n5.2\\\\nPrefetching and Overlapping\\\\nAlthough the unified memory pool mitigates fragmentation,\\\\nthe I/O overhead from loading and offloading remains a\\\\nconcern—especially when dealing with numerous or large\\\\nadapters. The latency introduced by waiting to load these\\\\nadapters can compromise the efficiency of the system.\\\\nTo proactively address this issue, we introduce a dynamic\\\\nprediction mechanism. While running the current decoding\\\\nbatch, we predict the adapters required for the next batch\\\\nbased on the current waiting queue. This prediction allows\\\\nus to prefetch and store them in available memory. Such a\\\\nforward-looking strategy keeps most of the adapters needed\\\\nfor the next batch already in place before running it, which\\\\nreduces I/O time for adapter swapping.\\\\n5.3\\\\nCustom Kernels for heterogeneous LoRA batching\\\\non Non-Contiguous Memory\\\\nDue to the design of the unified memory pool, the adapter\\\\nweights are stored in non-contiguous memory. To run com-\\\\nputations efficiently under this design, we implement cus-\\\\ntom CUDA kernels that support batching LoRA compu-\\\\ntations with varying ranks and sequence lengths in a non-\\\\ncontiguous memory layout. In the prefill stage, the kernel\\\\nhandles a sequence of tokens and gathers adapter weights\\\\nwith different ranks from the memory pool. We call this\\\\nkernel Multi-size Batched Gather Matrix-Matrix Multipli-\\\\ncation (MBGMM). It is implemented in Triton (Tillet et al.,\\\\n2019) with tiling. In the decode stage, the kernel handles\\\\na single token and gathers adapter weights with different\\\\nranks from the memory pool. We call this kernel Multi-size\\\\nBatched Gather Matrix-Vector Multiplication (MBGMV).\\\\nIt is modified from Punica (Chen, 2023) to support multiple\\\\nranks in a batch and more fine-grained memory gathering.\\\\n6\\\\nTENSOR PARALLELISM\\\\nWe design novel tensor parallelism strategies for batched\\\\nLoRA inference to support multi-GPU inference of large\\\\ntransformer models.\\\\nTensor parallelism is the most\\\\nwidely used parallelism method because its single-program\\\\nmultiple-data pattern simplifies its implementation and inte-\\\\ngration with existing systems. Tensor parallelism can reduce\\\\nthe per-GPU memory usage and latency when serving large\\\\nmodels. In our setting, the additional LoRA adapters intro-\\\\nduce new weight matrices and matrix multiplications, which\\\\ncalls for new partition strategies for these added items.\\\\n6.1\\\\nPartition Strategy\\\\nSince the base model uses the Megatron-LM tensor paral-\\\\nlelism strategy (Shoeybi et al., 2019), our approach aims\\\\nto align the partition strategies of inputs and outputs of the\\\\nadded LoRA computation with those of the base model.\\\\nIn this way, we can minimize the communication costs\\\\nby avoiding unnecessary communications and fusing some\\\\ncommunications.\\\\nWe use the feed-forward module (2-layer MLP) to illus-\\\\ntrate our partition strategy. We will explain later how this\\\\nstrategy can easily be adapted to the self-attention layer.\\\\nAs depicted in Figure 4, the upper box illustrates the base\\\\nmodel’s Megatron-LM partition strategy: the first weight\\\\nmatrix (W1) is column-partitioned, and the second (W2) is\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 6 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\ninput X\\\\nmatmul_1\\\\nmatmul_2\\\\nW1\\\\nW2\\\\nB1\\\\nadd_1\\\\nmatmul_3\\\\nB2\\\\nmatmul_4\\\\nall-reduce\\\\nadd_2\\\\nmatmul all-gather\\\\nmatmul all-reduce\\\\nA1\\\\nA2\\\\nColumn Partition\\\\nRow Partition\\\\nPartial Sum\\\\nReplication\\\\n(B, h)\\\\n(h, r/N)\\\\n(B, r/N)\\\\n(B, r)\\\\n(r, d/N)\\\\n(B, d/N)\\\\n(h, d/N)\\\\n(B, d/N)\\\\n(B, d/N)\\\\n(d/N, r)\\\\n(B, r)\\\\n(B, r)\\\\n(r, h/N)\\\\n(d/N, h)\\\\n(B, h)\\\\n(B, h/N)\\\\n(B, h)\\\\n(B, h)\\\\nFuse all-gather\\\\nand all-reduce\\\\nFigure 4. Tensor parallelism partition strategy for batched LoRA computation. This is a computational graph where nodes represent\\\\ntensors/operators and the edges represent dependency. We use different colors to represent different partition strategies, which include\\\\ncolumn partition, row partition, partial sum, and replication. The per-GPU shape of each tensor is also annotated in gray. Note that B is\\\\nthe number of tokens, h is the input dimension, N is the number of devices, d is the hidden size, and r is the adapter rank.\\\\nrow-partitioned. An all-reduce communication is required\\\\nto accumulate the partial sum from distributed devices.\\\\nThe lower box illustrates the partitioning strategy for the\\\\nadded LoRA computation. The matrices A1 and B1 for\\\\nthe adapter of the first weight matrix (W1) are column-\\\\npartitioned. An all-gather operation is used to collect the in-\\\\ntermediate results. The matrices A2 and B2 for the adapter\\\\nof the second weight (W2) are row-partitioned and column-\\\\npartitioned, respectively. An all-reduce operation is used\\\\nto sum up the intermediate results. Finally, the result from\\\\nthe LoRA computation is added to that from the base model\\\\n(add 2). A single all-reduce operation is sufficient to ac-\\\\ncumulate the final results. It is worth noting that we are\\\\nessentially fusing an all-gather operation for matmul 4\\\\nwith the final all-reduce. To our knowledge, this paralleliza-\\\\ntion strategy has not been studied before.\\\\nNext, we discuss adapting the strategy from the 2-layer MLP\\\\nto the self-attention layer. Similar to the Megatron-LM strat-\\\\negy, we partition the head dimension of the self-attention\\\\nlayer. The query-key-value projection weight matrix can be\\\\nseen as W1 in our example and the output projection weight\\\\nmatrix can be seen as W2 in our example.\\\\n6.2\\\\nCommunication and Memory Cost Analysis\\\\nLet N be the number of devices, B be the number of to-\\\\nkens, h be the hidden size, and r be the adapter rank. The\\\\ncommunication cost of the base model is one all-reduce, or\\\\n2(N−1)Bh\\\\nN\\\\n. The communication cost of the added LoRA\\\\ncomputation is three all-gather for query, key, and value\\\\nprojections, and one all-reduce for the output projection.\\\\nFormally, it is 3 (N−1)Br\\\\nN\\\\n+ 2(N−1)Br\\\\nN\\\\n= 5(N−1)Br\\\\nN\\\\n.\\\\nUnder our strategy, the additional communication cost intro-\\\\nduced by LoRA is negligible when compared to the commu-\\\\nnication cost of the base model, because r ≪h. Intuitively,\\\\nthis is achieved by carefully scheduling communications on\\\\nthe small intermediate tensors of LoRA computation and\\\\nfusing communications with base models.\\\\nIn terms of memory usage, our strategy is optimal because\\\\nwe partition all weight matrices among all devices and there\\\\nis no replicated weight matrix.\\\\n7\\\\nEVALUATION\\\\nWe evaluate the performance of S-LoRA on both synthetic\\\\nand real production workloads. This approach involves: 1) Updating the base\\\\nmodel with the current adapter weights before each new\\\\nbatch; and 2) Switching to a new adapter if there are too\\\\nmany waiting requests.2 This method is efficient for a small\\\\nnumber of adapters due to the reduced LoRA computation\\\\noverhead.\\\\nResults in Figure 9 demonstrate that with just one adapter,\\\\nthe merging approach outperforms the on-the-fly computa-\\\\ntion owing to a one-time merging cost. However, its per-\\\\nformance declines with more than 2 adapters, primarily\\\\nbecause of the time-consuming switch between adapters.\\\\nSuch switching results in periods of GPU under-utilization.\\\\nFurthermore, a smaller value of α causes requests to be\\\\ndistributed unevenly across adapters, which in turn reduces\\\\nbatch sizes and overall performance.\\\\nEarly abort strategy experiments.\\\\nWe compared S-\\\\nLoRA’s early abort strategy to First Come First Serve\\\\n(FCFS) and Last Come First Serve (LCFS) for optimiz-\\\\ning user satisfaction and SLO attainment. As shown in\\\\nFigure 10, S-LoRA-Abort outperforms both, especially as\\\\ncv scales. FCFS is least effective, often processing requests\\\\nthat have already missed the SLO. LCFS, similar to a greedy\\\\nalgorithm that only prioritizes the newest requests, works\\\\nwell for small cv, but its performance drops with larger\\\\n2This is different from PEFT. For example, it has continuous\\\\nbatching and PagedAttention, which are not enabled in PEFT.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 10 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n3\\\\n4\\\\n5\\\\nnumber of adapters\\\\n1.1\\\\n1.2\\\\n1.3\\\\n1.4\\\\n1.5\\\\n1.6\\\\n1.7\\\\n1.8\\\\nthroughput (req/s)\\\\nS-LoRA-merge alpha=0.1\\\\nS-LoRA alpha=0.1\\\\nS-LoRA-merge alpha=1\\\\nS-LoRA alpha=1\\\\nFigure 9.
