Gonzalez 1 Ion Stoica 1\\\\nABSTRACT\\\\nThe “pretrain-then-finetune” paradigm is commonly adopted in the deployment of large language models. Low-\\\\nRank Adaptation (LoRA), a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, is often employed to adapt a base model to a\\\\nmultitude of tasks, resulting in a substantial collection of LoRA adapters derived from one base model. We observe\\\\nthat this paradigm presents significant opportunities for batched inference during serving. To capitalize on these\\\\nopportunities, we present S-LoRA, a system designed for the scalable serving of many LoRA adapters. S-LoRA\\\\nstores all adapters in the main memory and fetches the adapters used by the currently running queries to the\\\\nGPU memory. To efficiently use the GPU memory and reduce fragmentation, S-LoRA proposes Unified Paging.\\\\nUnified Paging uses a unified memory pool to manage dynamic adapter weights with different ranks and KV cache\\\\ntensors with varying sequence lengths. Additionally, S-LoRA employs a novel tensor parallelism strategy and\\\\nhighly optimized custom CUDA kernels for heterogeneous batching of LoRA computation. Collectively, these\\\\nfeatures enable S-LoRA to serve thousands of LoRA adapters on a single GPU or across multiple GPUs with a\\\\nsmall overhead. Compared to state-of-the-art libraries such as HuggingFace PEFT and vLLM (with naive support\\\\nof LoRA serving), S-LoRA can improve the throughput by up to 4 times and increase the number of served\\\\nadapters by several orders of magnitude. As a result, S-LoRA enables scalable serving of many task-specific\\\\nfine-tuned models and offers the potential for large-scale customized fine-tuning services.\\\\n1\\\\nINTRODUCTION\\\\nLarge language models (LLMs) have become ubiquitous in\\\\nmodern applications, ranging from natural language pro-\\\\ncessing to more general tasks (OpenAI, 2023; Touvron\\\\net al., 2023b; Alayrac et al., 2022). Within these domains,\\\\nLLMs have consistently demonstrated superior performance,\\\\nespecially when fine-tuned for specific tasks (Kenton &\\\\nToutanova, 2019; Houlsby et al., 2019; Ouyang et al., 2022).\\\\nThis “pretrain-then-finetune” paradigm has led to the pro-\\\\nliferation of numerous fine-tuned variants of a single base\\\\nLLM, each tailored to a specific task or domain.\\\\nWhen scaling the fine-tuning of a base model for numerous\\\\ntasks, such as personalized assistants, the associated train-\\\\ning and serving costs can become substantial. To address\\\\nthis, several parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods have\\\\nbeen developed. A prime exemplar is Low-Rank Adaptation\\\\n(LoRA) (Hu et al., 2021), which enables efficient fine-tuning\\\\nby updating only low-rank additive matrices. These matri-\\\\nces consist of a small number of parameters, referred to as\\\\nadapter weights. LoRA has shown that by fine-tuning just\\\\n*Equal contribution. Part of the work was done when Ying\\\\nwas visiting UC Berkeley.\\\\n1UC Berkeley 2Stanford University\\\\n3Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Correspondence to: Ying Sheng\\\\n<ying1123@stanford.edu>, Shiyi Cao <shicao@berkeley.edu>.\\\\nthese adapter weights, it is possible to achieve performance\\\\non par with full-weight fine-tuning. However, despite con-\\\\nsiderable research into fine-tuning, the question of how to\\\\nserve these fine-tuned variants at scale remains unexplored.\\\\nOne of the key innovations in the LoRA paper was the\\\\nelimination of adapter inference latency by directly merging\\\\nthe adapter with the model parameters. Additionally, to\\\\nsupport multiple models on a single machine, the same\\\\npaper proposes swapping adapters by adding and subtracting\\\\nLoRA weights from the base model. While this approach\\\\nenables low-latency inference for a single adapter and serial\\\\nexecution across adapters, it significantly reduces overall\\\\nserving throughput and increases total latency when serving\\\\nmultiple adapters concurrently. Moreover, the paper does\\\\nnot consider the opportunity to leverage host memory to\\\\nincrease the number of adapters hosted by a single machine.\\\\nIn this paper, we study how to scalably serve thousands\\\\nof LoRA adapters on a single machine. We observe that\\\\nthe shared base model, which underpins numerous LoRA\\\\nadapters, presents a substantial opportunity for batched in-\\\\nference. To achieve high-throughput multi-adapter serving,\\\\nit is advantageous to separate the batchable base model\\\\ncomputation from individual LoRA computations.\\\\nWhile leveraging batching in the base model is straight-\\\\nforward (as all queries share the base model), extending\\\\narXiv:2311.03285v1  [cs.LG]  6 Nov 2023\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 2 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\nbatching to the adapters is challenging. First, serving many\\\\nLoRA adapters simultaneously requires efficient memory\\\\nmanagement. Since GPU memory is limited, we must store\\\\nadapter weights outside the GPU and dynamically fetch\\\\nthem when needed. However, dynamically loading and un-\\\\nloading adapters of varying sizes, coupled with the dynamic\\\\nallocation and deallocation of KV cache tensors for requests\\\\nwith different sequence lengths, can lead to significant mem-\\\\nory fragmentation and I/O overhead. Second, apart from\\\\nthe easily batchable base model computation, the separated\\\\ncomputation of many adapters with distinct ranks in non-\\\\ncontiguous memory is challenging to batch and demands the\\\\ndevelopment of new computation kernels. Third, leveraging\\\\nmultiple GPUs on a single machine requires novel paral-\\\\nlelism strategies to accommodate the added LoRA weights\\\\nand computations. It is essential to carefully design this strat-\\\\negy to minimize communication and memory overheads.\\\\nTo this end, we introduce S-LoRA, a scalable LoRA serving\\\\nsystem. S-LoRA exploits batching opportunities, efficiently\\\\nmanages both host and GPU memory, and orchestrates par-\\\\nallelism across multiple GPUs. The primary contributions\\\\nof S-LoRA are summarized as follows:\\\\n• Unified Paging: To reduce memory fragmentation and\\\\nincrease batch size, S-LoRA introduces a unified mem-\\\\nory pool. This pool manages dynamic adapter weights\\\\nand KV cache tensors by a unified paging mechanism.\\\\n• Heterogeneous Batching: To minimize the latency over-\\\\nhead when batching different adapters of varying ranks,\\\\nS-LoRA employs highly optimized custom CUDA ker-\\\\nnels. These kernels operate directly on non-contiguous\\\\nmemory and align with the memory pool design, fa-\\\\ncilitating efficient batched inference for added LoRA\\\\ncomputation.\\\\n• S-LoRA TP: To ensure effective parallelization across\\\\nmultiple GPUs, S-LoRA introduces a novel tensor par-\\\\nallelism strategy. This approach incurs minimal com-\\\\nmunication cost for the added LoRA computation com-\\\\npared to that of the base model. This is realized by\\\\nscheduling communications on small intermediate ten-\\\\nsors and fusing them with the communications of the\\\\nbase model.\\\\nWe evaluate S-LoRA by serving Llama-7B/13B/30B/70B.\\\\nResults show that S-LoRA can serve thousands of LoRA\\\\nadapters on a single GPU or across multiple GPUs with\\\\na small overhead. When compared to the state-of-the-art\\\\nparameter-efficient fine-tuning library, Huggingface PEFT,\\\\nS-LoRA can enhance throughput by up to 30×. In com-\\\\nparison to the high-throughput serving system vLLM using\\\\na naive support of LoRA serving, S-LoRA can improve\\\\nthroughput by up to 4× and increase the number of served\\\\nadapters by several orders of magnitude. The code is avail-\\\\nable at https://github.com/S-LoRA/S-LoRA.\\\\n2\\\\nBACKGROUND\\\\nLow-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2021) is a\\\\nparameter-efficient fine-tuning method designed to adapt\\\\npre-trained large language models to new tasks. The mo-\\\\ntivation behind LoRA stems from the low intrinsic dimen-\\\\nsionality of model updates during adaptation. In the training\\\\nphase, LoRA freezes the weights of a pre-trained base model\\\\nand adds trainable low-rank matrices to each layer. This\\\\napproach significantly reduces the number of trainable pa-\\\\nrameters and memory consumption. When compared to full\\\\nparameter fine-tuning, LoRA can often reduce the number of\\\\ntrainable parameters by orders of magnitude (e.g., 10000×)\\\\nwhile retaining comparable accuracy. For the inference\\\\nphase, the original paper suggests merging the low-rank\\\\nmatrices with the weights of the base model. As a result,\\\\nthere is no added overhead during inference, setting it apart\\\\nfrom previous adapters like (Houlsby et al., 2019) or prompt\\\\ntuning methods such as (Lester et al., 2021).\\\\nFormally, for a pre-trained weight matrix W ∈Rh×d, LoRA\\\\nintroduces the update as W ′ = W +AB, where A ∈Rh×r,\\\\nB ∈Rr×d, and the rank r ≪min(h, d). If the forward pass\\\\nof a base model is defined by h = xW, then after applying\\\\nLoRA, the forward pass becomes\\\\nh = xW ′ = x(W + AB)\\\\n(1)\\\\n= xW + xAB.\\\\n(2)\\\\nTypically, this adjustment is only applied to the query, key,\\\\nvalue, and output projection matrices in the self-attention\\\\nmodule, excluding the feed-forward module.\\\\nBecause LoRA greatly reduces the training and weight stor-\\\\nage costs, it has been widely adopted by the community,\\\\nand people have created hundreds of thousands of LoRA\\\\nadapters for pre-trained large language models and diffusion\\\\nmodels (Mangrulkar et al., 2022).\\\\n2.1\\\\nServing Large Language Models\\\\nMost large language models (LLMs) are based on the trans-\\\\nformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017). The number of\\\\nparameters in an LLM ranges from several billion to several\\\\ntrillion (Brown et al., 2020; Chowdhery et al., 2022; Fedus\\\\net al., 2022), corresponding to disk sizes spanning several gi-\\\\ngabytes to even terabytes. This scale results in LLM serving\\\\nhaving significant computational and memory demands.\\\\nAdditionally, the inference process for LLMs requires iter-\\\\native autoregressive decoding. Initially, the model carries\\\\nout a forward pass to encode the prompt. Following this, it\\\\ndecodes the output one token at a time. The sequential pro-\\\\ncess makes decoding slow. Since each token attends to the\\\\nhidden states of all its preceding tokens, it becomes essential\\\\nto store the hidden states of all previous tokens. This storage\\\\nis referred to as the “KV cache”. Such a mechanism adds to\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 3 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\nthe memory overhead and causes the decoding process to\\\\nbe more memory-intensive than computation-intensive.\\\\nThe challenges become even more pronounced in online\\\\nsettings, where requests of varying sequence lengths ar-\\\\nrive dynamically. To accommodate such dynamic incoming\\\\nrequests, Orca (Yu et al., 2022) introduces a method of fine-\\\\ngrained, iteration-level scheduling. Instead of scheduling at\\\\nthe request level, Orca batches at the token level. This ap-\\\\nproach allows for the continuous addition of new requests to\\\\nthe currently running batch, resulting in substantially higher\\\\nthroughput. vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) further optimizes\\\\nOrca’s memory efficiency using PagedAttention. PagedAt-\\\\ntention adopts concepts from virtual memory and paging in\\\\noperating systems and manages the storage and access of\\\\ndynamic KV cache tensors in a paged fashion. This method\\\\nefficiently reduces fragmentation, facilitating larger batch\\\\nsizes and higher throughput.\\\\nWhen serving very large models that exceed the memory\\\\ncapacity of a single GPU, or when there are stringent la-\\\\ntency requirements, it is necessary to parallelize the model\\\\nacross multiple GPUs. Several model parallelism methods\\\\nhave been proposed, such as tensor parallelism (Shoeybi\\\\net al., 2019), sequence parallelism (Korthikanti et al., 2023),\\\\npipeline parallelism (Huang et al., 2019), and their combi-\\\\nnations (Narayanan et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2022).\\\\n3\\\\nOVERVIEW OF S-LORA\\\\nS-LoRA encompasses three principal components of in-\\\\nnovation. In Section 4, we introduce our batching strat-\\\\negy, which decomposes the computation between the base\\\\nmodel and the LoRA adapters. Additionally, we address\\\\nthe challenge of request scheduling, covering aspects like\\\\nadapter clustering and admission control. The ability to\\\\nbatch across concurrent adapters, introduces new challenges\\\\naround memory management. In Section 5, we generalize\\\\nPagedAttention (Kwon et al., 2023) to Unfied Paging which\\\\nsupport dynamically loading LoRA adapters. This approach\\\\nuses a unified memory pool to store the KV caches and\\\\nadapter weights in a paged fashion, which can reduce frag-\\\\nmentation and balance the dynamic changing size of the\\\\nKV caches and adapter weights. Lastly, in Section 6, we\\\\nintroduce our new tensor parallelism strategy that enables us\\\\nto efficiently decoupled the base model and LoRA adapters.\\\\n4\\\\nBATCHING AND SCHEDULING\\\\n4.1\\\\nBatching\\\\nOur batching strategy aims to support online and high-\\\\nthroughput serving of many LoRA adapters simultaneously.\\\\nFor a single adapter, the method recommended by (Hu et al.,\\\\n2021) is to merge the adapter weights into the base model\\\\nW\\\\nx1\\\\nx2\\\\nx3\\\\nx\\\\nA\\\\n1\\\\nB1\\\\nx1\\\\nx\\\\nx\\\\nx2\\\\nA\\\\n2\\\\nB2\\\\nx\\\\nx\\\\nx3\\\\nA\\\\n3\\\\nB3\\\\nx\\\\nx\\\\nx\\\\nBatched base computation\\\\nBatched LoRA computation\\\\nadd\\\\nFigure 1. Separated batched computation for the base model and\\\\nLoRA computation. The batched computation of the base model\\\\nis implemented by GEMM. The batched computation for LoRA\\\\nadapters is implemented by custom CUDA kernels which support\\\\nbatching various sequence lengths and adapter ranks.\\\\nMain Memory\\\\nAdapter 1\\\\nAdapter 2\\\\nAdapter 3\\\\nAdapter 4\\\\nAdapter 5\\\\nAdapter 6\\\\n…\\\\nGPU Memory\\\\nKV cache\\\\nUnified memory pool\\\\nfor dynamic tensors\\\\nBase\\\\nModel\\\\nWeights\\\\nOther\\\\nTemporary\\\\nTensors\\\\nFetch active \\\\nadapters for\\\\nthe current batch\\\\nAdapter 2\\\\nAdapter 5\\\\nFigure 2. Overview of memory allocation in S-LoRA. S-LoRA\\\\nstores all adapters in the main memory and fetches the active\\\\nadapters for the current batch to the GPU memory. The GPU\\\\nmemory is used to store the KV cache, adapter weights, base\\\\nmodel weights, and other temporary tensors.\\\\nweights, resulting in a new model (see Eq. 1). This has the\\\\nadvantage that there is no additional adapter overhead during\\\\ninference, since the new model has the same number of\\\\nparameters as the base model. In fact, this was a prominent\\\\nfeature of the original LoRA work.\\\\nHowever, when there are multiple adapters, merging the\\\\nweights into the base model leads to multiple weight copies\\\\nand missed batching opportunities. Directly merging the\\\\nmodels requires maintaining many copies of the full lan-\\\\nguage model. In the original LoRA paper, the authors pro-\\\\nposed adding and subtracting LoRA weights on the fly to\\\\nenable serving multiple models without increasing the mem-\\\\nory overhead. However, this approach doesn’t support con-\\\\ncurrent inference on separate LoRA adapters and therefore\\\\nlimits batching opportunities.\\\\nIn this paper, we show that merging LoRA adapters into\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 4 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\nthe base model is inefficient for the multi-LoRA high-\\\\nthroughput serving setting. Instead, we propose computing\\\\nthe LoRA computation xAB on-the-fly as shown in Eq. 2.\\\\nThis avoids weight duplication and enables batching of the\\\\nmore costly xW operation. But this approach also increases\\\\nthe computation overhead. However, because the cost of\\\\nxAB is substantially lower than xW and there is a consid-\\\\nerable savings from batching xW across different adapters,\\\\nwe show that the savings far exceed the additional overhead.\\\\nUnfortunately, directly implementing the factored computa-\\\\ntion of the base model and individual LoRA adapters using\\\\nthe batch GEMM kernel from the existing BLAS libraries\\\\nwould require significant padding and result in poor hard-\\\\nware utilization. This is because of the heterogeneity of\\\\nsequence lengths and adapter ranks.\\\\nIn S-LoRA, we batch the computation of the base model and\\\\nthen employ custom CUDA kernels to execute the additional\\\\nxAB for all adapters separately. This process is illustrated\\\\nby Figure 1. Instead of naively using padding and using the\\\\nbatch GEMM kernel from the BLAS library for the LoRA\\\\ncomputation, we implement custom CUDA kernels for more\\\\nefficient computation without padding. In Subsection 5.3,\\\\nwe discuss the implementation details.\\\\nWhile the number of LoRA adapters can be large if we\\\\nstore them in main memory, the number of LoRA adapters\\\\nneeded for the currently running batch is manageable, be-\\\\ncause the batch size is bounded by the GPU memory. To\\\\ntake advantage of this, we store all LoRA adapters in the\\\\nmain memory and fetch only the LoRA adapters needed\\\\nfor the currently running batch to the GPU RAM when\\\\nrunning the inference for that batch. In this case, the max-\\\\nimum number of adapters that can be served is bounded\\\\nby the main memory size. This process is illustrated by\\\\nFigure 2. To achieve high-throughput serving, we adopt the\\\\niteration-level scheduling batching strategy from Orca (Yu\\\\net al., 2022). In this approach, requests are scheduled at the\\\\ntoken level. We immediately incorporate a new request into\\\\nthe running batch if space is available. The request will exit\\\\nthe batch once it reaches the maximum number of gener-\\\\nated tokens or fulfills other stopping criteria. This process\\\\nreduces GPU memory usage but introduces new memory\\\\nmanagement challenges. In Section 5, we will discuss our\\\\ntechniques to manage memory efficiently.\\\\n4.2\\\\nAdapter Clustering\\\\nTo enhance batching efficiency, one potential strategy is\\\\nreducing the number of active adapters in a running batch.\\\\nBy using fewer adapters, there is an opportunity to allocate\\\\nmore memory to the KV cache, which in turn can facili-\\\\ntate larger batch sizes. Given the common memory capaci-\\\\nties of GPUs, they are often underutilized while decoding.\\\\nConsequently, increasing the batch size can lead to higher\\\\nthroughput. A direct approach to reducing the number of\\\\nadapters in a running batch is to prioritize batching requests\\\\nthat use the same adapter, a strategy we term “adapter clus-\\\\ntering”. However, adapter clustering comes with its own set\\\\nof trade-offs. For example, it can hurt the average latency\\\\nor fairness among adapters. We provide an ablation study in\\\\nAppendix A to illustrate how throughput and latency change\\\\naccording to the cluster size.\\\\n4.3\\\\nAdmission Control\\\\nIn S-LoRA, we also applied an admission control strategy\\\\nto sustain good attainment when the traffic is higher than the\\\\nserving system capacity. A serving system is typically char-\\\\nacterized by a service level objective (SLO) which specifies\\\\nthe desired latency of processing requests. If the serving\\\\nsystem has fixed capacity, it must implement an admission\\\\ncontrol mechanism, that drops a request, if the system can-\\\\nnot meet its SLO. Otherwise, if no request is dropped, and\\\\nthe number of incoming requests is larger than the system\\\\ncapacity for long enough, the serving system is bound to\\\\nviolate the SLO. We implemented an abort strategy to mimic\\\\nadmission control in S-LoRA, called early abort strategy.\\\\nIntuitively, we estimate the set of latest requests that we\\\\ncan serve in SLO, and then serve them in the order of ar-\\\\nrival time. More implementation details and mathematical\\\\njustifications are deferred to Appendix B.\\\\n5\\\\nMEMORY MANAGEMENT\\\\nCompared to serving a single base model, serving multiple\\\\nLoRA adapters simultaneously presents new memory man-\\\\nagement challenges. To support many adapters, S-LoRA\\\\nstores them in the main memory and dynamically loads the\\\\nadapter weights needed for the currently running batch into\\\\nGPU RAM. During this process, there are two noticeable\\\\nchallenges. The first is memory fragmentation, resulting\\\\nfrom the dynamic loading and offloading adapter weights of\\\\nvarious sizes. The second is the latency overhead introduced\\\\nby adapter loading and offloading. To tackle these chal-\\\\nlenges efficiently, we propose Unfied Paging and overlap\\\\nthe I/O with computation by prefetching adapter weights.\\\\n5.1\\\\nUnified Paging\\\\nUnderstanding the nature of adapter weights is essential for\\\\noptimizing memory usage. Our primary observation is that\\\\nthese dynamic adapter weights are analogous to dynamic\\\\nKV caches in several ways:\\\\n• Variable sizes and operations: Just as the size of\\\\nKV cache size fluctuates with the sequence length, the\\\\nranks of the active adapters can also depend on the\\\\nchoice of adapter associated with each request. KV\\\\ncaches are allocated when requests arrive and deal-\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 5 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\nKV caches\\\\nAdapter weights\\\\nEmpty\\\\nH\\\\nFigure 3. Unified memory pool. We use a unified memory pool to\\\\nstore both KV caches and adapter weights in a non-contiguous way\\\\nto reduce memory fragmentation. The page size is H elements.\\\\nlocated once the requests are completed. Similarly,\\\\nadapter weights are loaded and cleared with each re-\\\\nquest. If not managed properly, this variability can\\\\nresult in fragmentation.\\\\n• Dimensionality: A KV cache tensor for a request in\\\\na layer has a shape of (S, H), where S denotes the se-\\\\nquence length and H represents the hidden dimension.\\\\nMeanwhile, the shape of a LoRA weight is (R, H),\\\\nwith R standing for the rank and H the hidden dimen-\\\\nsion. Both share a dimension size of H that can be\\\\nleveraged to reduce fragmentation.\\\\nMotivated by these parallels, we extend the idea of Page-\\\\ndAttention (Kwon et al., 2023) to Unified Paging which\\\\nmanages adapter weights in addition to the KV cache. Uni-\\\\nfied Paging uses a unified memory pool to jointly manage\\\\nboth KV cache and adapter weights. To implement this, we\\\\nfirst allocate a large buffer statically for the memory pool.\\\\nThis buffer uses all available space except for the space oc-\\\\ncupied by the base model weights and temporary activation\\\\ntensors. Both KV caches and adapter weights are stored in\\\\nthis memory pool in a paged manner, with each page corre-\\\\nsponding to a vector of H. Thus, a KV cache tensor with a\\\\nsequence length of S uses up S pages, while a LoRA weight\\\\ntensor of rank R takes up R pages. Figure 3 illustrates the\\\\nlayout of our memory pool, where KV caches and adapter\\\\nweights are stored interleaved and non-contiguously. This\\\\napproach significantly reduces fragmentation, ensuring that\\\\nadapters weights of various ranks can coexist with dynamic\\\\nKV caches in a structured and systematic manner.\\\\n5.2\\\\nPrefetching and Overlapping\\\\nAlthough the unified memory pool mitigates fragmentation,\\\\nthe I/O overhead from loading and offloading remains a\\\\nconcern—especially when dealing with numerous or large\\\\nadapters. The latency introduced by waiting to load these\\\\nadapters can compromise the efficiency of the system.\\\\nTo proactively address this issue, we introduce a dynamic\\\\nprediction mechanism. While running the current decoding\\\\nbatch, we predict the adapters required for the next batch\\\\nbased on the current waiting queue. This prediction allows\\\\nus to prefetch and store them in available memory. Such a\\\\nforward-looking strategy keeps most of the adapters needed\\\\nfor the next batch already in place before running it, which\\\\nreduces I/O time for adapter swapping.\\\\n5.3\\\\nCustom Kernels for heterogeneous LoRA batching\\\\non Non-Contiguous Memory\\\\nDue to the design of the unified memory pool, the adapter\\\\nweights are stored in non-contiguous memory. To run com-\\\\nputations efficiently under this design, we implement cus-\\\\ntom CUDA kernels that support batching LoRA compu-\\\\ntations with varying ranks and sequence lengths in a non-\\\\ncontiguous memory layout. In the prefill stage, the kernel\\\\nhandles a sequence of tokens and gathers adapter weights\\\\nwith different ranks from the memory pool. We call this\\\\nkernel Multi-size Batched Gather Matrix-Matrix Multipli-\\\\ncation (MBGMM). It is implemented in Triton (Tillet et al.,\\\\n2019) with tiling. In the decode stage, the kernel handles\\\\na single token and gathers adapter weights with different\\\\nranks from the memory pool. We call this kernel Multi-size\\\\nBatched Gather Matrix-Vector Multiplication (MBGMV).\\\\nIt is modified from Punica (Chen, 2023) to support multiple\\\\nranks in a batch and more fine-grained memory gathering.\\\\n6\\\\nTENSOR PARALLELISM\\\\nWe design novel tensor parallelism strategies for batched\\\\nLoRA inference to support multi-GPU inference of large\\\\ntransformer models.\\\\nTensor parallelism is the most\\\\nwidely used parallelism method because its single-program\\\\nmultiple-data pattern simplifies its implementation and inte-\\\\ngration with existing systems. Tensor parallelism can reduce\\\\nthe per-GPU memory usage and latency when serving large\\\\nmodels. In our setting, the additional LoRA adapters intro-\\\\nduce new weight matrices and matrix multiplications, which\\\\ncalls for new partition strategies for these added items.\\\\n6.1\\\\nPartition Strategy\\\\nSince the base model uses the Megatron-LM tensor paral-\\\\nlelism strategy (Shoeybi et al., 2019), our approach aims\\\\nto align the partition strategies of inputs and outputs of the\\\\nadded LoRA computation with those of the base model.\\\\nIn this way, we can minimize the communication costs\\\\nby avoiding unnecessary communications and fusing some\\\\ncommunications.\\\\nWe use the feed-forward module (2-layer MLP) to illus-\\\\ntrate our partition strategy. We will explain later how this\\\\nstrategy can easily be adapted to the self-attention layer.\\\\nAs depicted in Figure 4, the upper box illustrates the base\\\\nmodel’s Megatron-LM partition strategy: the first weight\\\\nmatrix (W1) is column-partitioned, and the second (W2) is\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 6 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\ninput X\\\\nmatmul_1\\\\nmatmul_2\\\\nW1\\\\nW2\\\\nB1\\\\nadd_1\\\\nmatmul_3\\\\nB2\\\\nmatmul_4\\\\nall-reduce\\\\nadd_2\\\\nmatmul all-gather\\\\nmatmul all-reduce\\\\nA1\\\\nA2\\\\nColumn Partition\\\\nRow Partition\\\\nPartial Sum\\\\nReplication\\\\n(B, h)\\\\n(h, r/N)\\\\n(B, r/N)\\\\n(B, r)\\\\n(r, d/N)\\\\n(B, d/N)\\\\n(h, d/N)\\\\n(B, d/N)\\\\n(B, d/N)\\\\n(d/N, r)\\\\n(B, r)\\\\n(B, r)\\\\n(r, h/N)\\\\n(d/N, h)\\\\n(B, h)\\\\n(B, h/N)\\\\n(B, h)\\\\n(B, h)\\\\nFuse all-gather\\\\nand all-reduce\\\\nFigure 4. The query-key-value projection weight matrix can be\\\\nseen as W1 in our example and the output projection weight\\\\nmatrix can be seen as W2 in our example.\\\\n6.2\\\\nCommunication and Memory Cost Analysis\\\\nLet N be the number of devices, B be the number of to-\\\\nkens, h be the hidden size, and r be the adapter rank. The\\\\ncommunication cost of the base model is one all-reduce, or\\\\n2(N−1)Bh\\\\nN\\\\n. The communication cost of the added LoRA\\\\ncomputation is three all-gather for query, key, and value\\\\nprojections, and one all-reduce for the output projection.\\\\nFormally, it is 3 (N−1)Br\\\\nN\\\\n+ 2(N−1)Br\\\\nN\\\\n= 5(N−1)Br\\\\nN\\\\n.\\\\nUnder our strategy, the additional communication cost intro-\\\\nduced by LoRA is negligible when compared to the commu-\\\\nnication cost of the base model, because r ≪h. Intuitively,\\\\nthis is achieved by carefully scheduling communications on\\\\nthe small intermediate tensors of LoRA computation and\\\\nfusing communications with base models.\\\\nIn terms of memory usage, our strategy is optimal because\\\\nwe partition all weight matrices among all devices and there\\\\nis no replicated weight matrix.\\\\n7\\\\nEVALUATION\\\\nWe evaluate the performance of S-LoRA on both synthetic\\\\nand real production workloads. The model and hardware\\\\nconfiguration is S2 on an A10G (24GB).\\\\n7.3\\\\nEnd-to-End Results on Real Workloads\\\\nReal workload trace. We construct real-world serving\\\\ntraces by downsampling from the traces of LMSYS Chatbot\\\\nArena (Zheng et al., 2023b;a), a website that serves multiple\\\\nLLMs. The raw log from Arena does not concern LoRA\\\\nadapters; it focuses on different base models. Nonetheless,\\\\nwe treat the distribution of different base models as if they\\\\nwere the distribution of different adapters of a single base\\\\nmodel. The raw log can be sampled into traces that exhibit\\\\nvarying request rates, denoted as R, and durations, repre-\\\\nsented by D. To achieve this, we sample R · D requests\\\\nfrom the raw log and rescale the time stamps to fit within\\\\nthe range of [0, D]. The number of models n corresponds\\\\nto the number of adapters. Furthermore, we set the adapter\\\\nranks based on Table 1 with a round-robin method.\\\\nSince we are using a real workload trace, there are no pa-\\\\nrameters such as α, λi, or cv. For consistency, we set the\\\\nduration to 5 minutes. We adjust the request rate R to study\\\\nits impact on performance metrics. In the sampled trace, the\\\\naverage input length is 85 tokens, the average output length\\\\nis 165 tokens, and the number of adapters is around 26.\\\\nResults. Figure 7 shows the throughput and attainment\\\\nresults, which show a similar pattern to the synthetic work-\\\\nloads. This means the strong performance S-LoRA holds\\\\nfor real world workloads.\\\\n7.4\\\\nMulti-GPU Tensor Parallelism\\\\nWe test the scalability of our tensor parallelism strategy by\\\\nrunning 1) Llama-30B on two A100 (40GB) and four A100\\\\n(40GB) GPUs with 10 to 100 adapters; and 2) Llama-70B\\\\non two A100 (80GB) and four A100 (80GB) GPUs with 10\\\\nadapters. We then report the serving throughputs.\\\\nAs depicted in Figure 8, the disparity between S-LoRA\\\\nwith and without LoRA communication is small. This sug-\\\\ngests that the added LoRA communication in our strategy\\\\nhas a very small overhead. The figure further reveals that\\\\nthe communication overhead due to LoRA is less than the\\\\ncomputational overhead it introduces. Furthermore, when\\\\ntransitioning from 2 GPUs to 4 GPUs, the serving through-\\\\nput increases by more than 2 times. This significant increase\\\\ncan be attributed to the fact that the system is predominantly\\\\nmemory-bound in this context. Adding more GPUs alle-\\\\nviates memory constraints, leading to superlinear scaling.\\\\nIn conclusion, the results verify both the minimal overhead\\\\nand the scalability of our tensor parallelism strategy.\\\\nLlama-30B\\\\n2xA100(40GB)\\\\nn=10\\\\nLlama-30B\\\\n2xA100(40GB)\\\\nn=10\\\\n0\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n3\\\\n4\\\\n5\\\\nThroughput (req/s)\\\\nS-LoRA\\\\nS-LoRA (w/o LoRA communication)\\\\nS-LoRA (base only)\\\\nLlama-30B\\\\n2xA100(40GB)\\\\nn=100\\\\nLlama-30B\\\\n4xA100(40GB)\\\\nn=100\\\\n0\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n3\\\\n4\\\\n5\\\\nLlama-70B\\\\n2xA100(80GB)\\\\nn=10\\\\nLlama-70B\\\\n4xA100(80GB)\\\\nn=10\\\\n0.0\\\\n0.5\\\\n1.0\\\\n1.5\\\\n2.0\\\\n2.5\\\\n3.0\\\\n3.5\\\\nFigure 8. Throughput with tensor parallelism.\\\\n7.5\\\\nAblation Study\\\\nMerging adapter weights versus computing on-the-fly.\\\\nWhile S-LoRA does not merge adapter weights and com-\\\\nputes LoRA matrices on-the-fly each time, we compare it\\\\nwith an alternative design that merges an adapter with the\\\\nbase model, denoted as x(W + AB), as proposed in the\\\\nLoRA paper. This approach involves: 1) Updating the base\\\\nmodel with the current adapter weights before each new\\\\nbatch; and 2) Switching to a new adapter if there are too\\\\nmany waiting requests.2 This method is efficient for a small\\\\nnumber of adapters due to the reduced LoRA computation\\\\noverhead.\\\\nResults in Figure 9 demonstrate that with just one adapter,\\\\nthe merging approach outperforms the on-the-fly computa-\\\\ntion owing to a one-time merging cost. However, its per-\\\\nformance declines with more than 2 adapters, primarily\\\\nbecause of the time-consuming switch between adapters.\\\\nSuch switching results in periods of GPU under-utilization.\\\\nFurthermore, a smaller value of α causes requests to be\\\\ndistributed unevenly across adapters, which in turn reduces\\\\nbatch sizes and overall performance.\\\\nEarly abort strategy experiments.\\\\nWe compared S-\\\\nLoRA’s early abort strategy to First Come First Serve\\\\n(FCFS) and Last Come First Serve (LCFS) for optimiz-\\\\ning user satisfaction and SLO attainment. As shown in\\\\nFigure 10, S-LoRA-Abort outperforms both, especially as\\\\ncv scales. FCFS is least effective, often processing requests\\\\nthat have already missed the SLO. LCFS, similar to a greedy\\\\nalgorithm that only prioritizes the newest requests, works\\\\nwell for small cv, but its performance drops with larger\\\\n2This is different from PEFT. For example, it has continuous\\\\nbatching and PagedAttention, which are not enabled in PEFT.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 10 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n3\\\\n4\\\\n5\\\\nnumber of adapters\\\\n1.1\\\\n1.2\\\\n1.3\\\\n1.4\\\\n1.5\\\\n1.6\\\\n1.7\\\\n1.8\\\\nthroughput (req/s)\\\\nS-LoRA-merge alpha=0.1\\\\nS-LoRA alpha=0.1\\\\nS-LoRA-merge alpha=1\\\\nS-LoRA alpha=1\\\\nFigure 9. S-LoRA-Abort excels as it avoids prioritizing only the\\\\nnewest requests, as detailed in Appendix B.\\\\n8\\\\nRELATED WORK\\\\nOptimize LLM serving with system techniques. The sig-\\\\nnificance of the transformer architecture has led to the devel-\\\\nopment of many specialized serving systems for it. These\\\\nsystems use advanced batching mechanisms (Fang et al.,\\\\n2021; Yu et al., 2022), memory optimizations (Sheng et al.,\\\\n2023; Kwon et al., 2023), GPU kernel optimizations (Wang\\\\net al., 2021; Aminabadi et al., 2022; NVIDIA, 2023; Dao,\\\\n2023), model parallelism (Pope et al., 2022; Aminabadi\\\\net al., 2022), parameter sharing (Zhou et al., 2022), and\\\\nspeculative execution (Stern et al., 2018; Miao et al., 2023)\\\\nfor efficient serving. Among them, PetS (Zhou et al., 2022)\\\\nis most relevant to ours. However, PetS only considers\\\\nthe serving for small encoder-only BERT models. It does\\\\nnot consider generative inference, a very large number of\\\\nadapters or large models go beyond a single GPU, so it does\\\\nnot address the problems in our settings.\\\\nIn a concurrent work (Chen et al., 2023), the concept of\\\\ndecomposed computation for the base model and adapters\\\\nwas explored. Our CUDA kernels were developed based\\\\non the implementation presented in a prior blog post of this\\\\nstudy, with additional support for batching different ranks\\\\nand non-contiguous memory. Moreover, our novel memory\\\\nmanagement and tensor parallelism techniques have not\\\\nbeen covered in any previous work.\\\\nOptimize LLM serving with algorithm techniques. In\\\\naddition to system-level improvements, inference efficiency\\\\ncan be enhanced using algorithm techniques like quanti-\\\\nzation (Yao et al., 2022; Dettmers et al., 2022; Frantar\\\\net al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2023), sparsifi-\\\\ncation (Frantar & Alistarh, 2023; Zhang et al., 2023b) and\\\\nmodel architecture improvements (Shazeer, 2019). These\\\\napproaches can reduce memory consumption and accelerate\\\\nthe computation, with a minor compromise in model quality.\\\\nThey are complementary to the techniques in this paper.\\\\nParameter-efficient fine-tuning. Recent work has devel-\\\\noped methods for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large\\\\npre-trained language models. These methods show fine-\\\\ntuning is possible with only a small fraction of tuned param-\\\\neters. The state-of-the-art methods include LoRA (Hu et al.,\\\\n2021), Prefix-tuning (Li & Liang, 2021), P-Tuning (Liu\\\\net al., 2021), Prompt tuning (Liu et al., 2023; Lester et al.,\\\\n2021), AdaLoRA (Zhang et al., 2022), and (IA)3 (Liu et al.,\\\\n2022). While our paper focuses on LoRA due to its wide\\\\nadoption, most techniques can be easily applied to other\\\\nparameter-efficient fine-tuning methods as well.\\\\nGeneral purpose model serving systems. Over the years,\\\\nthe domain of general model serving has seen significant\\\\nadvancements, Notable systems from earlier research in-\\\\nclude Clipper (Crankshaw et al., 2017), TensorFlow Serv-\\\\ning (Olston et al., 2017), Nexus (Shen et al., 2019), Infer-\\\\nLine (Crankshaw et al., 2020), and Clockwork (Gujarati\\\\net al., 2020). These systems delve into topics such as batch-\\\\ning, caching, and model placement, catering to both individ-\\\\nual and multiple model deployments. In more recent devel-\\\\nopments, DVABatch (Cui et al., 2022), REEF (Han et al.,\\\\n2022), Shepherd (Zhang et al., 2023a) and AlpaServe (Li\\\\net al., 2023) have explored the ideas of multi-entry multi-\\\\nexit batching, preemption, and statistical multiplexing with\\\\nmodel parallelism. Although these systems have made sig-\\\\nnificant contributions, they overlook the auto-regressive\\\\ncharacteristics and parameter-efficient adapters in LLM serv-\\\\ning, leading to potential optimization gaps.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 11 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\n9\\\\nCONCLUSION\\\\nWe present S-LoRA, a system capable of serving thou-\\\\nsands of LoRA adapters from a single machine with much\\\\nhigher throughput compared to existing systems. S-LoRA\\\\nis made possible by our innovative design of the unified\\\\nmemory pool, tensor parallelism strategy, adapter batch-\\\\ning, and CUDA kernels. S-LoRA enables large-scale, cus-\\\\ntomized fine-tuning services essential for deploying models\\\\ntailored to diverse requirements. Future extensions of S-\\\\nLoRA will encompass support for additional adapter meth-\\\\nods, enhanced fused kernels, and the use of multiple CUDA\\\\nstreams to parallelize base model and LoRA computations.\\\\n10\\\\nACKNOWLEDGMENT\\\\nThis research was supported by gifts from Anyscale, As-\\\\ntronomer, Google, IBM, Intel, Lacework, Microsoft, Mo-\\\\nhamed Bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, Sam-\\\\nsung SDS, Uber, and VMware. Here for LoRA\\\\nserving, we assume a soft threshold characterized by the\\\\nuser’s reward function. For illustration purposes, let the\\\\narrival time of the requests be integers, and assume that\\\\nwe process one query in each time period of length 1. Let\\\\nQ = {q1, q2, · · · qn} be the request queue in the ascending\\\\norder of the arrival time, and l be the desired number of\\\\nserved requests. We quantify the user’s satisfaction with a\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n=== PDF page 16 ===\\\\nS-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters\\\\nreward function r : R+ 7→[0, 1] that maps the first token\\\\nlatency of a request to a scalar in between [0, 1], where 0\\\\nrepresents the user losing patience and giving up the query,\\\\nand 1 represents the user is completely satisfied with the\\\\nlatency. Let ti be the latency of serving the request qi in the\\\\nqueue Q. Then we aim to solve the following constrained\\\\noptimization:\\\\nmax\\\\nn\\\\nX\\\\ni=1\\\\nr(ti)\\\\n(3)\\\\ns.t. 1(r(ti) > 0) = l.\\\\nWe show that when the derivative of reward is non-\\\\nincreasing, the optimal solution to the above constrained\\\\noptimization problem is to serve the most recent l elements\\\\nqn−l+1, qn−l+2, · · · , qn in order.\\\\nTheorem B.1. Assume that r′(t) ≤0 for any t ∈R+. The\\\\noptimal solution to Equation (3) is to serve the most recent\\\\nl elements qn−l+1, qn−l+2, · · · , qn in order.\\\\nThe proof is deferred to Appendix B.1. In practice, for a\\\\ngiven request queue, we can estimate the largest possible\\\\nnumber of requests to be served in SLO as l. Then we\\\\ntake the most recent l elements for serving. Such an l can\\\\nbe approximated by simulating a First-Come-First-Serve\\\\n(FCFS) strategy, which is optimized to serve requests as\\\\nmany as possible.\\\\nIn S-LoRA, the scenario is more complicated because of the\\\\nheterogeneity and unpredictability of the sequence length.\\\\nAs an approximation, we implement a heuristic as follows.\\\\nThe high-level scheduling is that we will fetch a minibatch\\\\nof new requests to be added into the running batch every\\\\nseveral decode step. From the history, we use the moving\\\\naverage to estimate a current request rate R1 measured in\\\\nhow many requests will be added to the waiting queue per\\\\nperiod of fetching new requests. We also use the moving\\\\naverage to estimate the number of new requests R2 that can\\\\nbe added to the running batch for a period. Let rti be the\\\\ncoming time of request ri, ct be the current time, tlmax be\\\\nthe maximum allowed first token latency to meet the SLO\\\\nand lprefill be the maximum prefill latency for a minibatch\\\\nin history. Each time we generate the new minibatch, we\\\\nwill first abort the requests R = {rk | ct −rtk + lprefill >\\\\ntlmax}. Requests in R are highly likely to miss the SLO\\\\neven if they get scheduled immediately due to the high\\\\nprefill latency. Then if R1 > R2, which means the system\\\\nis temporarily overloaded, we will fetch the newest requests\\\\ninto the minibatch. If R1 ≤R2, the waiting queue will be\\\\nshortened if the trend continues. In this case, we will choose\\\\nfrom the earliest.\\\\nB.1\\\\nProof of Theorem B.1\\\\nWe first prove that for any admission control strategy that\\\\nserves l elements, one can always find another admission\\\\ncontrol strategy that serves the most recent l elements with\\\\na larger cumulative reward.\\\\nAssume that we serve l elements qs1, qs2, · · · , qsl in the l\\\\ntimesteps. Assume without loss of generality that qs1 is not\\\\namong the most recent l elements, and assume that the k-th\\\\nelement is not served with k ∈[n −l, n]. By definition\\\\nwe know that s1 < k. Now at the time of serving qs1, we\\\\nserve qk rather than qs1, and keep the rest of the choices in\\\\nother time steps same. In this case, the number of served\\\\nqueries remains the same. On the other hand, we know that\\\\nthe latency satisfies ts1 > tk since the k-th element is more\\\\nrecent. This gives that\\\\nr(ts1) < r(tk).\\\\nSince the reward for other elements does not change, the\\\\ntotal reward is increased while the constraint is still satisfied.\\\\nBy repeating the operations until all the elements served are\\\\nthe most recent l elements, we prove that claim.\\\\nNext, we prove that serving the most recent l elements in\\\\norder of qn−l+1, qn−l+2, · · · , qn is optimal. For any i, j ∈\\\\n[n −l + 1, n], we assume that i < j and j is first served at\\\\ntime t1 while i is served at time t2 with t1 < t2. Let ta\\\\ni , ta\\\\nj\\\\nbe the arrival time of i, j. The reward for serving i, j in this\\\\ncase becomes\\\\nr(t2 −ta\\\\ni ) + r(t1 −ta\\\\nj ).\\\\nNow we show that by swapping the time of serving i, j, the\\\\nreward does not decrease. This is equivalent to showing that\\\\nr(t1 −ta\\\\ni ) + r(t2 −ta\\\\nj ) ≥r(t2 −ta\\\\ni ) + r(t1 −ta\\\\nj ).\\\\nRearranging the above equation, we know that it is equiva-\\\\nlent to\\\\nr(t1 −ta\\\\ni ) −r(t2 −ta\\\\ni )\\\\nt1 −t2\\\\n≤r(t1 −ta\\\\nj ) −r(t2 −ta\\\\nj )\\\\nt1 −t2\\\\n.\\\\nThis is true due to the concavity of the reward function, thus\\\\nfinishing the proof.\\\\n\\\", \\\"excerpt_ranges\\\": [[0, 70861]], \\\"range_unit\\\": \\\"zero-based half-open characters in extracted text\\\", \\\"extracted_characters\\\": 70861, \\\"selected_characters\\\": 70861, \\\"extraction\\\": \\\"UTF-8 text\\\", \\\"selection_reason\\\": \\\"full extracted text fits allocation\\\"}, {\\\"path\\\": \\\"references/S-LORA/fulltext.txt\\\", \\\"sha256\\\": \\\"8bdfe54c7a265b4fe33ba00f96d9979d6416ca5348d416eedb597170899d40ea\\\", \\\"reading_scope\\\": \\\"full\\\", \\\"category\\\": \\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"--- PAGE 1 ---\\\\nLORA: LOW-RANK ADAPTATION OF LARGE LAN-\\\\nGUAGE MODELS\\\\nEdward Hu∗\\\\nYelong Shen∗\\\\nPhillip Wallis\\\\nZeyuan Allen-Zhu\\\\nYuanzhi Li\\\\nShean Wang\\\\nLu Wang\\\\nWeizhu Chen\\\\nMicrosoft Corporation\\\\n{edwardhu, yeshe, phwallis, zeyuana,\\\\nyuanzhil, swang, luw, wzchen}@microsoft.com\\\\nyuanzhil@andrew.cmu.edu\\\\n(Version 2)\\\\nABSTRACT\\\\nAn important paradigm of natural language processing consists of large-scale pre-\\\\ntraining on general domain data and adaptation to particular tasks or domains. As\\\\nwe pre-train larger models, full ﬁne-tuning, which retrains all model parameters,\\\\nbecomes less feasible. Using GPT-3 175B as an example – deploying indepen-\\\\ndent instances of ﬁne-tuned models, each with 175B parameters, is prohibitively\\\\nexpensive. We propose Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, which freezes the pre-\\\\ntrained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each\\\\nlayer of the Transformer architecture, greatly reducing the number of trainable pa-\\\\nrameters for downstream tasks. Compared to GPT-3 175B ﬁne-tuned with Adam,\\\\nLoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the\\\\nGPU memory requirement by 3 times. LoRA performs on-par or better than ﬁne-\\\\ntuning in model quality on RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2, and GPT-3, despite hav-\\\\ning fewer trainable parameters, a higher training throughput, and, unlike adapters,\\\\nno additional inference latency. We also provide an empirical investigation into\\\\nrank-deﬁciency in language model adaptation, which sheds light on the efﬁcacy of\\\\nLoRA. We release a package that facilitates the integration of LoRA with PyTorch\\\\nmodels and provide our implementations and model checkpoints for RoBERTa,\\\\nDeBERTa, and GPT-2 at https://github.com/microsoft/LoRA.\\\\n1\\\\nINTRODUCTION\\\\nPretrained \\\\nWeights\\\\n𝑊∈ℝ𝑑×𝑑\\\\nx\\\\nh\\\\n𝐵= 0\\\\n𝐴= 𝒩(0, 𝜎2)\\\\n𝑑\\\\n𝑟\\\\nFigure 1: Our reparametriza-\\\\ntion. We only train A and B.\\\\nMany applications in natural language processing rely on adapt-\\\\ning one large-scale, pre-trained language model to multiple down-\\\\nstream applications. Such adaptation is usually done via ﬁne-tuning,\\\\nwhich updates all the parameters of the pre-trained model. The ma-\\\\njor downside of ﬁne-tuning is that the new model contains as many\\\\nparameters as in the original model. As larger models are trained\\\\nevery few months, this changes from a mere “inconvenience” for\\\\nGPT-2 (Radford et al., b) or RoBERTa large (Liu et al., 2019) to a\\\\ncritical deployment challenge for GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) with\\\\n175 billion trainable parameters.1\\\\nMany sought to mitigate this by adapting only some parameters or\\\\nlearning external modules for new tasks. This way, we only need\\\\nto store and load a small number of task-speciﬁc parameters in ad-\\\\ndition to the pre-trained model for each task, greatly boosting the\\\\noperational efﬁciency when deployed. However, existing techniques\\\\n∗Equal contribution.\\\\n0Compared to V1, this draft includes better baselines, experiments on GLUE, and more on adapter latency.\\\\n1While GPT-3 175B achieves non-trivial performance with few-shot learning, ﬁne-tuning boosts its perfor-\\\\nmance signiﬁcantly as shown in Appendix A.\\\\n1\\\\narXiv:2106.09685v2  [cs.CL]  16 Oct 2021\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 2 ---\\\\noften introduce inference latency (Houlsby et al., 2019; Rebufﬁet al., 2017) by extending model\\\\ndepth or reduce the model’s usable sequence length (Li & Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Ham-\\\\nbardzumyan et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021) (Section 3). More importantly, these method often fail to\\\\nmatch the ﬁne-tuning baselines, posing a trade-off between efﬁciency and model quality.\\\\nWe take inspiration from Li et al. (2018a); Aghajanyan et al. (2020) which show that the learned\\\\nover-parametrized models in fact reside on a low intrinsic dimension. We hypothesize that the\\\\nchange in weights during model adaptation also has a low “intrinsic rank”, leading to our proposed\\\\nLow-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) approach. LoRA allows us to train some dense layers in a neural\\\\nnetwork indirectly by optimizing rank decomposition matrices of the dense layers’ change during\\\\nadaptation instead, while keeping the pre-trained weights frozen, as shown in Figure 1. Using GPT-3\\\\n175B as an example, we show that a very low rank (i.e., r in Figure 1 can be one or two) sufﬁces even\\\\nwhen the full rank (i.e., d) is as high as 12,288, making LoRA both storage- and compute-efﬁcient.\\\\nLoRA possesses several key advantages.\\\\n• A pre-trained model can be shared and used to build many small LoRA modules for dif-\\\\nferent tasks. We can freeze the shared model and efﬁciently switch tasks by replacing the\\\\nmatrices A and B in Figure 1, reducing the storage requirement and task-switching over-\\\\nhead signiﬁcantly.\\\\n• LoRA makes training more efﬁcient and lowers the hardware barrier to entry by up to 3\\\\ntimes when using adaptive optimizers since we do not need to calculate the gradients or\\\\nmaintain the optimizer states for most parameters. Instead, we only optimize the injected,\\\\nmuch smaller low-rank matrices.\\\\n• Our simple linear design allows us to merge the trainable matrices with the frozen weights\\\\nwhen deployed, introducing no inference latency compared to a fully ﬁne-tuned model, by\\\\nconstruction.\\\\n• LoRA is orthogonal to many prior methods and can be combined with many of them, such\\\\nas preﬁx-tuning. We provide an example in Appendix E.\\\\nTerminologies and Conventions\\\\nWe make frequent references to the Transformer architecture\\\\nand use the conventional terminologies for its dimensions.\\\\nWe call the input and output di-\\\\nmension size of a Transformer layer dmodel.\\\\nWe use Wq, Wk, Wv, and Wo to refer to the\\\\nquery/key/value/output projection matrices in the self-attention module. W or W0 refers to a pre-\\\\ntrained weight matrix and ∆W its accumulated gradient update during adaptation. We use r to\\\\ndenote the rank of a LoRA module. We follow the conventions set out by (Vaswani et al., 2017;\\\\nBrown et al., 2020) and use Adam (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019; Kingma & Ba, 2017) for model\\\\noptimization and use a Transformer MLP feedforward dimension dffn = 4 × dmodel.\\\\n2\\\\nPROBLEM STATEMENT\\\\nWhile our proposal is agnostic to training objective, we focus on language modeling as our motivat-\\\\ning use case. Below is a brief description of the language modeling problem and, in particular, the\\\\nmaximization of conditional probabilities given a task-speciﬁc prompt.\\\\nSuppose we are given a pre-trained autoregressive language model PΦ(y|x) parametrized by Φ.\\\\nFor instance, PΦ(y|x) can be a generic multi-task learner such as GPT (Radford et al., b; Brown\\\\net al., 2020) based on the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017). Consider adapting this\\\\npre-trained model to downstream conditional text generation tasks, such as summarization, machine\\\\nreading comprehension (MRC), and natural language to SQL (NL2SQL). Each downstream task is\\\\nrepresented by a training dataset of context-target pairs: Z = {(xi, yi)}i=1,..,N, where both xi and\\\\nyi are sequences of tokens. For example, in NL2SQL, xi is a natural language query and yi its\\\\ncorresponding SQL command; for summarization, xi is the content of an article and yi its summary.\\\\n2\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 3 ---\\\\nDuring full ﬁne-tuning, the model is initialized to pre-trained weights Φ0 and updated to Φ0 + ∆Φ\\\\nby repeatedly following the gradient to maximize the conditional language modeling objective:\\\\nmax\\\\nΦ\\\\nX\\\\n(x,y)∈Z\\\\n|y|\\\\nX\\\\nt=1\\\\nlog (PΦ(yt|x, y<t))\\\\n(1)\\\\nOne of the main drawbacks for full ﬁne-tuning is that for each downstream task, we learn a different\\\\nset of parameters ∆Φ whose dimension |∆Φ| equals |Φ0|. Thus, if the pre-trained model is large\\\\n(such as GPT-3 with |Φ0| ≈175 Billion), storing and deploying many independent instances of\\\\nﬁne-tuned models can be challenging, if at all feasible.\\\\nIn this paper, we adopt a more parameter-efﬁcient approach, where the task-speciﬁc parameter\\\\nincrement ∆Φ = ∆Φ(Θ) is further encoded by a much smaller-sized set of parameters Θ with\\\\n|Θ| ≪|Φ0|. The task of ﬁnding ∆Φ thus becomes optimizing over Θ:\\\\nmax\\\\nΘ\\\\nX\\\\n(x,y)∈Z\\\\n|y|\\\\nX\\\\nt=1\\\\nlog\\\\n\\\\u0000pΦ0+∆Φ(Θ)(yt|x, y<t)\\\\n\\\\u0001\\\\n(2)\\\\nIn the subsequent sections, we propose to use a low-rank representation to encode ∆Φ that is both\\\\ncompute- and memory-efﬁcient. When the pre-trained model is GPT-3 175B, the number of train-\\\\nable parameters |Θ| can be as small as 0.01% of |Φ0|.\\\\n3\\\\nAREN’T EXISTING SOLUTIONS GOOD ENOUGH?\\\\nThe problem we set out to tackle is by no means new. Since the inception of transfer learning, dozens\\\\nof works have sought to make model adaptation more parameter- and compute-efﬁcient. See Sec-\\\\ntion 6 for a survey of some of the well-known works. Using language modeling as an example, there\\\\nare two prominent strategies when it comes to efﬁcient adaptations: adding adapter layers (Houlsby\\\\net al., 2019; Rebufﬁet al., 2017; Pfeiffer et al., 2021; R¨uckl´e et al., 2020) or optimizing some forms\\\\nof the input layer activations (Li & Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Hambardzumyan et al., 2020;\\\\nLiu et al., 2021). However, both strategies have their limitations, especially in a large-scale and\\\\nlatency-sensitive production scenario.\\\\nAdapter Layers Introduce Inference Latency\\\\nThere are many variants of adapters. We focus\\\\non the original design by Houlsby et al. (2019) which has two adapter layers per Transformer block\\\\nand a more recent one by Lin et al. (2020) which has only one per block but with an additional\\\\nLayerNorm (Ba et al., 2016). While one can reduce the overall latency by pruning layers or exploit-\\\\ning multi-task settings (R¨uckl´e et al., 2020; Pfeiffer et al., 2021), there is no direct ways to bypass\\\\nthe extra compute in adapter layers. This seems like a non-issue since adapter layers are designed\\\\nto have few parameters (sometimes <1% of the original model) by having a small bottleneck di-\\\\nmension, which limits the FLOPs they can add. However, large neural networks rely on hardware\\\\nparallelism to keep the latency low, and adapter layers have to be processed sequentially. This makes\\\\na difference in the online inference setting where the batch size is typically as small as one. In a\\\\ngeneric scenario without model parallelism, such as running inference on GPT-2 (Radford et al., b)\\\\nmedium on a single GPU, we see a noticeable increase in latency when using adapters, even with a\\\\nvery small bottleneck dimension (Table 1).\\\\nThis problem gets worse when we need to shard the model as done in Shoeybi et al. (2020); Lep-\\\\nikhin et al. (2020), because the additional depth requires more synchronous GPU operations such as\\\\nAllReduce and Broadcast, unless we store the adapter parameters redundantly many times.\\\\nDirectly Optimizing the Prompt is Hard\\\\nThe other direction, as exempliﬁed by preﬁx tuning (Li\\\\n& Liang, 2021), faces a different challenge. We observe that preﬁx tuning is difﬁcult to optimize\\\\nand that its performance changes non-monotonically in trainable parameters, conﬁrming similar\\\\nobservations in the original paper. More fundamentally, reserving a part of the sequence length for\\\\nadaptation necessarily reduces the sequence length available to process a downstream task, which\\\\nwe suspect makes tuning the prompt less performant compared to other methods. We defer the study\\\\non task performance to Section 5.\\\\n3\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 4 ---\\\\nBatch Size\\\\n32\\\\n16\\\\n1\\\\nSequence Length\\\\n512\\\\n256\\\\n128\\\\n|Θ|\\\\n0.5M\\\\n11M\\\\n11M\\\\nFine-Tune/LoRA\\\\n1449.4±0.8\\\\n338.0±0.6\\\\n19.8±2.7\\\\nAdapterL\\\\n1482.0±1.0 (+2.2%)\\\\n354.8±0.5 (+5.0%)\\\\n23.9±2.1 (+20.7%)\\\\nAdapterH\\\\n1492.2±1.0 (+3.0%)\\\\n366.3±0.5 (+8.4%)\\\\n25.8±2.2 (+30.3%)\\\\nTable 1: Infernece latency of a single forward pass in GPT-2 medium measured in milliseconds, av-\\\\neraged over 100 trials. AdapterL and AdapterH are two variants of adapter tuning, which we\\\\ndescribe in Section 5.1. The inference latency introduced by adapter layers can be signiﬁcant in an\\\\nonline, short-sequence-length scenario. See the full study in Appendix B.\\\\n4\\\\nOUR METHOD\\\\nWe describe the simple design of LoRA and its practical beneﬁts. The principles outlined here apply\\\\nto any dense layers in deep learning models, though we only focus on certain weights in Transformer\\\\nlanguage models in our experiments as the motivating use case.\\\\n4.1\\\\nLOW-RANK-PARAMETRIZED UPDATE MATRICES\\\\nA neural network contains many dense layers which perform matrix multiplication. The weight\\\\nmatrices in these layers typically have full-rank. When adapting to a speciﬁc task, Aghajanyan et al.\\\\n(2020) shows that the pre-trained language models have a low “instrisic dimension” and can still\\\\nlearn efﬁciently despite a random projection to a smaller subspace. Inspired by this, we hypothe-\\\\nsize the updates to the weights also have a low “intrinsic rank” during adaptation. For a pre-trained\\\\nweight matrix W0 ∈Rd×k, we constrain its update by representing the latter with a low-rank de-\\\\ncomposition W0 + ∆W = W0 + BA, where B ∈Rd×r, A ∈Rr×k, and the rank r ≪min(d, k).\\\\nDuring training, W0 is frozen and does not receive gradient updates, while A and B contain trainable\\\\nparameters. Note both W0 and ∆W = BA are multiplied with the same input, and their respective\\\\noutput vectors are summed coordinate-wise. For h = W0x, our modiﬁed forward pass yields:\\\\nh = W0x + ∆Wx = W0x + BAx\\\\n(3)\\\\nWe illustrate our reparametrization in Figure 1. We use a random Gaussian initialization for A and\\\\nzero for B, so ∆W = BA is zero at the beginning of training. We then scale ∆Wx by α\\\\nr , where α\\\\nis a constant in r. When optimizing with Adam, tuning α is roughly the same as tuning the learning\\\\nrate if we scale the initialization appropriately. As a result, we simply set α to the ﬁrst r we try\\\\nand do not tune it. This scaling helps to reduce the need to retune hyperparameters when we vary\\\\nr (Yang & Hu, 2021).\\\\nA Generalization of Full Fine-tuning.\\\\nA more general form of ﬁne-tuning allows the training of\\\\na subset of the pre-trained parameters. LoRA takes a step further and does not require the accumu-\\\\nlated gradient update to weight matrices to have full-rank during adaptation. This means that when\\\\napplying LoRA to all weight matrices and training all biases2, we roughly recover the expressive-\\\\nness of full ﬁne-tuning by setting the LoRA rank r to the rank of the pre-trained weight matrices. In\\\\nother words, as we increase the number of trainable parameters 3, training LoRA roughly converges\\\\nto training the original model, while adapter-based methods converges to an MLP and preﬁx-based\\\\nmethods to a model that cannot take long input sequences.\\\\nNo Additional Inference Latency.\\\\nWhen deployed in production, we can explicitly compute and\\\\nstore W = W0 + BA and perform inference as usual. Note that both W0 and BA are in Rd×k.\\\\nWhen we need to switch to another downstream task, we can recover W0 by subtracting BA and\\\\nthen adding a different B′A′, a quick operation with very little memory overhead. Critically, this\\\\n2They represent a negligible number of parameters compared to weights.\\\\n3An inevitability when adapting to hard tasks.\\\\n4\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 5 ---\\\\nguarantees that we do not introduce any additional latency during inference compared to a ﬁne-tuned\\\\nmodel by construction.\\\\n4.2\\\\nAPPLYING LORA TO TRANSFORMER\\\\nIn principle, we can apply LoRA to any subset of weight matrices in a neural network to reduce the\\\\nnumber of trainable parameters. In the Transformer architecture, there are four weight matrices in\\\\nthe self-attention module (Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo) and two in the MLP module. We treat Wq (or Wk, Wv)\\\\nas a single matrix of dimension dmodel ×dmodel, even though the output dimension is usually sliced\\\\ninto attention heads. We limit our study to only adapting the attention weights for downstream\\\\ntasks and freeze the MLP modules (so they are not trained in downstream tasks) both for simplicity\\\\nand parameter-efﬁciency.We further study the effect on adapting different types of attention weight\\\\nmatrices in a Transformer in Section 7.1. We leave the empirical investigation of adapting the MLP\\\\nlayers, LayerNorm layers, and biases to a future work.\\\\nPractical Beneﬁts and Limitations.\\\\nThe most signiﬁcant beneﬁt comes from the reduction in\\\\nmemory and storage usage. For a large Transformer trained with Adam, we reduce that VRAM\\\\nusage by up to 2/3 if r ≪dmodel as we do not need to store the optimizer states for the frozen\\\\nparameters. On GPT-3 175B, we reduce the VRAM consumption during training from 1.2TB to\\\\n350GB. With r = 4 and only the query and value projection matrices being adapted, the checkpoint\\\\nsize is reduced by roughly 10,000× (from 350GB to 35MB)4. This allows us to train with signiﬁ-\\\\ncantly fewer GPUs and avoid I/O bottlenecks. Another beneﬁt is that we can switch between tasks\\\\nwhile deployed at a much lower cost by only swapping the LoRA weights as opposed to all the\\\\nparameters. This allows for the creation of many customized models that can be swapped in and out\\\\non the ﬂy on machines that store the pre-trained weights in VRAM. We also observe a 25% speedup\\\\nduring training on GPT-3 175B compared to full ﬁne-tuning5 as we do not need to calculate the\\\\ngradient for the vast majority of the parameters.\\\\nLoRA also has its limitations. For example, it is not straightforward to batch inputs to different tasks\\\\nwith different A and B in a single forward pass, if one chooses to absorb A and B into W to eliminate\\\\nadditional inference latency. Though it is possible to not merge the weights and dynamically choose\\\\nthe LoRA modules to use for samples in a batch for scenarios where latency is not critical.\\\\n5\\\\nEMPIRICAL EXPERIMENTS\\\\nWe evaluate the downstream task performance of LoRA on RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), De-\\\\nBERTa (He et al., 2021), and GPT-2 (Radford et al., b), before scaling up to GPT-3 175B (Brown\\\\net al., 2020). Our experiments cover a wide range of tasks, from natural language understanding\\\\n(NLU) to generation (NLG). Speciﬁcally, we evaluate on the GLUE (Wang et al., 2019) benchmark\\\\nfor RoBERTa and DeBERTa. We follow the setup of Li & Liang (2021) on GPT-2 for a direct com-\\\\nparison and add WikiSQL (Zhong et al., 2017) (NL to SQL queries) and SAMSum (Gliwa et al.,\\\\n2019) (conversation summarization) for large-scale experiments on GPT-3. See Appendix C for\\\\nmore details on the datasets we use. (2019) for a fair comparison.\\\\nBias-only or BitFit is a baseline where we only train the bias vectors while freezing everything else.\\\\nContemporarily, this baseline has also been studied by BitFit (Zaken et al., 2021).\\\\nPreﬁx-embedding tuning (PreEmbed) inserts special tokens among the input tokens. These spe-\\\\ncial tokens have trainable word embeddings and are generally not in the model’s vocabulary. Where\\\\nto place such tokens can have an impact on performance. We focus on “preﬁxing”, which prepends\\\\nsuch tokens to the prompt, and “inﬁxing”, which appends to the prompt; both are discussed in Li &\\\\nLiang (2021). We use lp (resp. li) denote the number of preﬁx (resp. inﬁx) tokens. The number of\\\\ntrainable parameters is |Θ| = dmodel × (lp + li).\\\\nPreﬁx-layer tuning (PreLayer) is an extension to preﬁx-embedding tuning. The resulting number of trainable parameters is\\\\n|Θ| = L × dmodel × (lp + li), where L is the number of Transformer layers.\\\\nAdapter tuning as proposed in Houlsby et al. LoRA exhibits better scalability and task performance.\\\\nSee Section F.2 for more details on the plotted data points.\\\\n6\\\\nRELATED WORKS\\\\nTransformer Language Models.\\\\nTransformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) is a sequence-to-sequence\\\\narchitecture that makes heavy use of self-attention. Radford et al. (a) applied it to autoregressive lan-\\\\nguage modeling by using a stack of Transformer decoders. Since then, Transformer-based language\\\\nmodels have dominated NLP, achieving the state-of-the-art in many tasks. A new paradigm emerged\\\\nwith BERT (Devlin et al., 2019b) and GPT-2 (Radford et al., b) – both are large Transformer lan-\\\\n8\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 9 ---\\\\nguage models trained on a large amount of text – where ﬁne-tuning on task-speciﬁc data after pre-\\\\ntraining on general domain data provides a signiﬁcant performance gain compared to training on\\\\ntask-speciﬁc data directly. Training larger Transformers generally results in better performance and\\\\nremains an active research direction. GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) is the largest single Transformer\\\\nlanguage model trained to-date with 175B parameters.\\\\nPrompt Engineering and Fine-Tuning.\\\\nWhile GPT-3 175B can adapt its behavior with just a\\\\nfew additional training examples, the result depends heavily on the input prompt (Brown et al.,\\\\n2020). This necessitates an empirical art of composing and formatting the prompt to maximize a\\\\nmodel’s performance on a desired task, which is known as prompt engineering or prompt hacking.\\\\nFine-tuning retrains a model pre-trained on general domains to a speciﬁc task Devlin et al. (2019b);\\\\nRadford et al. (a). Variants of it include learning just a subset of the parameters Devlin et al. (2019b);\\\\nCollobert & Weston (2008), yet practitioners often retrain all of them to maximize the downstream\\\\nperformance. However, the enormity of GPT-3 175B makes it challenging to perform ﬁne-tuning in\\\\nthe usual way due to the large checkpoint it produces and the high hardware barrier to entry since it\\\\nhas the same memory footprint as pre-training.\\\\nParameter-Efﬁcient Adaptation.\\\\nMany have proposed inserting adapter layers between existing\\\\nlayers in a neural network (Houlsby et al., 2019; Rebufﬁet al., 2017; Lin et al., 2020). Our method\\\\nuses a similar bottleneck structure to impose a low-rank constraint on the weight updates. The\\\\nkey functional difference is that our learned weights can be merged with the main weights during\\\\ninference, thus not introducing any latency, which is not the case for the adapter layers (Section 3).\\\\nA comtenporary extension of adapter is COMPACTER (Mahabadi et al., 2021), which essentially\\\\nparametrizes the adapter layers using Kronecker products with some predetermined weight sharing\\\\nscheme. Similarly, combining LoRA with other tensor product-based methods could potentially\\\\nimprove its parameter efﬁciency, which we leave to future work. More recently, many proposed\\\\noptimizing the input word embeddings in lieu of ﬁne-tuning, akin to a continuous and differentiable\\\\ngeneralization of prompt engineering (Li & Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Hambardzumyan et al.,\\\\n2020; Liu et al., 2021). We include comparisons with Li & Liang (2021) in our experiment section.\\\\nHowever, this line of works can only scale up by using more special tokens in the prompt, which\\\\ntake up available sequence length for task tokens when positional embeddings are learned.\\\\nLow-Rank Structures in Deep Learning.\\\\nLow-rank structure is very common in machine learn-\\\\ning. A lot of machine learning problems have certain intrinsic low-rank structure (Li et al., 2016;\\\\nCai et al., 2010; Li et al., 2018b; Grasedyck et al., 2013). Moreover, it is known that for many\\\\ndeep learning tasks, especially those with a heavily over-parametrized neural network, the learned\\\\nneural network will enjoy low-rank properties after training (Oymak et al., 2019). Some prior works\\\\neven explicitly impose the low-rank constraint when training the original neural network (Sainath\\\\net al., 2013; Povey et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2014; Jaderberg et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2016; Kho-\\\\ndak et al., 2021; Denil et al., 2014); however, to the best of our knowledge, none of these works\\\\nconsiders low-rank update to a frozen model for adaptation to downstream tasks. In theory liter-\\\\nature, it is known that neural networks outperform other classical learning methods, including the\\\\ncorresponding (ﬁnite-width) neural tangent kernels (Allen-Zhu et al., 2019; Li & Liang, 2018) when\\\\nthe underlying concept class has certain low-rank structure (Ghorbani et al., 2020; Allen-Zhu & Li,\\\\n2019; Allen-Zhu & Li, 2020a). Another theoretical result in Allen-Zhu & Li (2020b) suggests that\\\\nlow-rank adaptations can be useful for adversarial training. In sum, we believe that our proposed\\\\nlow-rank adaptation update is well-motivated by the literature.\\\\n7\\\\nUNDERSTANDING THE LOW-RANK UPDATES\\\\nGiven the empirical advantage of LoRA, we hope to further explain the properties of the low-rank\\\\nadaptation learned from downstream tasks. Note that the low-rank structure not only lowers the\\\\nhardware barrier to entry which allows us to run multiple experiments in parallel, but also gives\\\\nbetter interpretability of how the update weights are correlated with the pre-trained weights. We\\\\nfocus our study on GPT-3 175B, where we achieved the largest reduction of trainable parameters\\\\n(up to 10,000×) without adversely affecting task performances.\\\\nWe perform a sequence of empirical studies to answer the following questions: 1) Given a parameter\\\\nbudget constraint, which subset of weight matrices in a pre-trained Transformer should we adapt\\\\n9\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 10 ---\\\\nto maximize downstream performance? 2) Is the “optimal” adaptation matrix ∆W really rank-\\\\ndeﬁcient? If so, what is a good rank to use in practice? 3) What is the connection between ∆W and\\\\nW? Does ∆W highly correlate with W? How large is ∆W comparing to W?\\\\nWe believe that our answers to question (2) and (3) shed light on the fundamental principles of using\\\\npre-trained language models for downstream tasks, which is a critical topic in NLP.\\\\n7.1\\\\nWHICH WEIGHT MATRICES IN TRANSFORMER SHOULD WE APPLY LORA TO?\\\\nGiven a limited parameter budget, which types of weights should we adapt with LoRA to obtain\\\\nthe best performance on downstream tasks? As mentioned in Section 4.2, we only consider weight\\\\nmatrices in the self-attention module. We propose\\\\nLoRA, an efﬁcient adaptation strategy that neither introduces inference latency nor reduces input\\\\nsequence length while retaining high model quality. Importantly, it allows for quick task-switching\\\\nwhen deployed as a service by sharing the vast majority of the model parameters. While we focused\\\\non Transformer language models, the proposed principles are generally applicable to any neural\\\\nnetworks with dense layers.\\\\nThere are many directions for future works. 1) LoRA can be combined with other efﬁcient adapta-\\\\ntion methods, potentially providing orthogonal improvement. 2) The mechanism behind ﬁne-tuning\\\\nor LoRA is far from clear – how are features learned during pre-training transformed to do well\\\\non downstream tasks? We believe that LoRA makes it more tractable to answer this than full ﬁne-\\\\n12\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 13 ---\\\\ntuning. 3) We mostly depend on heuristics to select the weight matrices to apply LoRA to. Are\\\\nthere more principled ways to do it? 4) Finally, the rank-deﬁciency of ∆W suggests that W could\\\\nbe rank-deﬁcient as well, which can also be a source of inspiration for future works.\\\\nREFERENCES\\\\nArmen Aghajanyan, Luke Zettlemoyer, and Sonal Gupta. URL http://\\\\narxiv.org/abs/1709.00103.\\\\nA\\\\nLARGE LANGUAGE MODELS STILL NEED PARAMETER UPDATES\\\\nFew-shot learning, or prompt engineering, is very advantageous when we only have a handful of\\\\ntraining samples. However, in practice, we can often afford to curate a few thousand or more training\\\\nexamples for performance-sensitive applications. As shown in Table 8, ﬁne-tuning improves the\\\\nmodel performance drastically compared to few-shot learning on datasets large and small. Consequently,\\\\nadapter layers must be computed in addition to the base model, inevitably introducing additional\\\\nlatency. While as pointed out in R¨uckl´e et al. (2020), the latency introduced by adapter layers can\\\\nbe mitigated when the model batch size and/or sequence length is large enough to full utilize the\\\\nhardware parallelism. We conﬁrm their observation with a similar latency study on GPT-2 medium\\\\nand point out that there are scenarios, notably online inference where the batch size is small, where\\\\nthe added latency can be signiﬁcant.\\\\nWe measure the latency of a single forward pass on an NVIDIA Quadro RTX8000 by averaging\\\\nover 100 trials. We vary the input batch size, sequence length, and the adapter bottleneck dimension\\\\nr. We test two adapter designs: the original one by Houlsby et al. (2019), which we call AdapterH,\\\\nand a recent, more efﬁcient variant by Lin et al. (2020), which we call AdapterL. See Section 5.1\\\\nfor more details on the designs. We plot the slow-down in percentage compared to the no-adapter\\\\nbaseline in Figure 5.\\\\n0\\\\n5\\\\n10\\\\n15\\\\n20\\\\n25\\\\n30\\\\n35\\\\n0\\\\n10\\\\n100\\\\n250\\\\nAdapterH r\\\\nSeq Len = 128\\\\nSeq Len = 256\\\\nSeq Len = 512\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\n16\\\\n32\\\\nBatch Size\\\\n0\\\\n10\\\\n100\\\\n250\\\\nAdapterL r\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\n16\\\\n32\\\\nBatch Size\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n4\\\\n8\\\\n16\\\\n32\\\\nBatch Size\\\\nFigure 5: Percentage slow-down of inference latency compared to the no-adapter (r = 0) baseline.\\\\nThe top row shows the result for AdapterH and the bottom row AdapterL. We tweak the colormap for better visibility.\\\\nC\\\\nDATASET DETAILS\\\\nGLUE Benchmark is a wide-ranging collection of natural language understanding tasks. It includes\\\\nMNLI (inference, Williams et al. (2018)), SST-2 (sentiment analysis, Socher et al. (2013)), MRPC\\\\n(paraphrase detection, Dolan & Brockett (2005)), CoLA (linguistic acceptability, Warstadt et al.\\\\n(2018)), QNLI (inference, Rajpurkar et al. (2018)), QQP8 (question-answering), RTE (inference),\\\\n8https://quoradata.quora.com/First-Quora-Dataset-Release-Question-Pairs\\\\n17\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 18 ---\\\\nand STS-B (textual similarity, Cer et al. (2017)). The broad coverage makes GLUE benchmark a\\\\nstandard metric to evaluate NLU models such as RoBERTa and DeBERTa. The individual datasets\\\\nare released under different permissive licenses.\\\\nWikiSQL is introduced in Zhong et al. (2017) and contains 56, 355/8, 421 training/validation ex-\\\\namples. The task is to generate SQL queries from natural language questions and table schemata.\\\\nWe encode context as x = {table schema, query} and target as y = {SQL}. The dataset is release\\\\nunder the BSD 3-Clause License.\\\\nSAMSum is introduced in Gliwa et al. (2019) and contains 14, 732/819 training/test examples. It\\\\nconsists of staged chat conversations between two people and corresponding abstractive summaries\\\\nwritten by linguists. We encode context as ”\\\\\\\\n” concatenated utterances followed by a ”\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n”,\\\\nand target as y = {summary}. The dataset is released under the non-commercial licence: Creative\\\\nCommons BY-NC-ND 4.0.\\\\nE2E NLG Challenge was ﬁrst introduced in Novikova et al. (2017) as a dataset for training end-to-\\\\nend, data-driven natural language generation systems and is commonly used for data-to-text evalua-\\\\ntion. The E2E dataset consists of roughly 42, 000 training, 4, 600 validation, and 4, 600 test exam-\\\\nples from the restaurant domain. Each source table used as input can have multiple references. Each\\\\nsample input (x, y) consists of a sequence of slot-value pairs, along with a corresponding natural\\\\nlanguage reference text. The dataset is released under Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 4.0.\\\\nDART is an open-domain data-to-text dataset described in Nan et al. (2020). DART inputs are\\\\nstructured as sequences of ENTITY — RELATION — ENTITY triples. With 82K examples in\\\\ntotal, DART is a signiﬁcantly larger and more complex data-to-text task compared to E2E. The\\\\ndataset is released under the MIT license.\\\\nWebNLG is another commonly used dataset for data-to-text evaluation (Gardent et al., 2017). With\\\\n22K examples in total WebNLG comprises 14 distinct categories, nine of which are seen during\\\\ntraining. Since ﬁve of the 14 total categories are not seen during training, but are represented in\\\\nthe test set, evaluation is typically broken out by “seen” categories (S), “unseen” categories (U)\\\\nand “all” (A). Each input example is represented by a sequence of SUBJECT — PROPERTY —\\\\nOBJECT triples. The dataset is released under Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 4.0.\\\\nD\\\\nHYPERPARAMETERS USED IN EXPERIMENTS\\\\nD.1\\\\nROBERTA\\\\nWe train using AdamW with a linear learning rate decay schedule.
